description: Interrupt Magma while it is running (no prompt visible) to obtain a new prompt. Magma interrupts at a convenient point. If typed twice within half a second, Magma exits immediately.
Terminate the current Magma session.
Terminate the current Magma session (same effect as `quit;`).
Immediately quit Magma by sending SIGQUIT to the process (Unix). Useful when `<Ctrl>-C` is unresponsive.
Assign the value of expression `e` to identifier `x`.
Assign the first `n` of `m ≥ n` values returned by `e` to `x1, ..., xn` respectively.
Evaluate `e` and discard its return value(s).
Expression returning `true` if the local identifier `x` currently has an assigned value, `false` otherwise. Returns `false` for intrinsic function names (not local variables).
Access and modify the entry of `x` (which must support at least `n` levels of indexing) indicated by the expressions `e1, ..., en`. Equivalent to the comma-separated form.
Equivalent comma-separated form of indexed assignment. Most important case is (nested) sequences.

If the right-hand side returns a structure supporting named generators (finitely generated groups, algebras, polynomial rings, etc.), assign the first `n` generator names to `x1, ..., xn` for both printing and as variable bindings. Equivalent to `E := e; x1 := E.1; ...` plus the print-name side effect.

If the right-hand side returns a structure `S` supporting named generators, assign names formed by appending `1, 2, ...` (in brackets) to the string `x`, and assign `x` to the sequence of generator names of `S`.

Procedure. For a structure `S` that supports named generators, reassign generator print-names to the strings `s1, ..., sn`. The length of the sequence must match the number of generators. Creates a new structure.

Mutation (in-place) assignment: evaluates `e`, applies operator `o` to the result and the current value of `x`, and reassigns `x`. Equivalent to (but an optimised form of) `x := x o e;`. Supported operators: `join`, `meet`, `diff`, `sdiff`, `cat`, `*`, `+`, `-`, `/`, `^`, `div`, `mod`, `and`, `or`, `xor`.

Statement. Delete the current value of identifier `x`, freeing memory (unless other variables still reference it). If `x` previously shadowed an intrinsic function, the intrinsic is restored. Intrinsic functions themselves cannot be deleted.
Return the Boolean structure `B`.
Cardinality of the Boolean structure (always 2).
The Boolean element true.
The Boolean element false.
Return a random Boolean element.
Returns `true` if both `x` and `y` are true. If `x` is `false`, `y` is not evaluated.
Returns `true` if `x` or `y` (or both) is true. If `x` is `true`, `y` is not evaluated.
Returns `true` if exactly one of `x`, `y` is true.
Negate the truth value of `x`.
If `x` and `y` are comparable, return `true` iff `x = y`; otherwise raise an error. Recommended for general use so type errors are caught.
If `x` and `y` are comparable, return `true` iff `x ≠ y`; otherwise raise an error.
If `x` and `y` are comparable, return whether `x = y`; otherwise return `false`. Never raises an error. Use when comparing objects of completely different types where no error is desired.
If `x` and `y` are comparable, return whether `x ≠ y`; otherwise return `true`. Never raises an error.
Attempt to coerce object `x` into structure `S`; return the result if successful. Raise an error if the coercion fails.
Attempt to coerce `x` into `S`; return `true` and the coerced element if successful, otherwise return `false`.

Expression that temporarily binds identifier `id` to the value of `e2`, then evaluates and returns `e1`. Scope of `id` is the `where` construction alone (unless inside an expression list or set/sequence constructor — see below). The token `:=` is a synonym for `is`.
Synonym for the `is` form above.

signature: `if Boolean expression then statements1 else statements2 end if;`
description: Evaluate the Boolean expression; if true execute `statements1`, otherwise execute `statements2`.

signature: `if Boolean expression then statements end if;`
description: Abbreviated form with no else branch.

signature: `if Boolean expression1 then statements1 elif Boolean expression2 then statements2 else statements3 end if;`
description: `elif` is a convenient abbreviation for `else if`, restricting nesting level. Multiple `elif` branches are allowed.
An expression whose value is `expression1` if the Boolean is true, otherwise `expression2`. Particularly important for in-line conditionals inside set and sequence constructors. Nesting is allowed.

signature: `case expression : when expression, ..., expression: statements ... else: statements end case;`
description: Evaluate the `case` expression. Execute the statements following the first `when` expression list that contains a matching value; then exit. If no match, execute the `else` branch (which may be omitted if no action is desired).

signature: `case< expression | expressionleft,1 : expressionright,1, ..., expressionleft,n : expressionright,n, default : expressiondef >`
description: Expression form of `case`. Evaluates the discriminant to value `v`; evaluates each left-hand expression in order until one equals `v`, then returns the corresponding right-hand expression. If no match, returns `expressiondef`. The `default` case is mandatory and must come last.

Construct an error object with user-defined payload `x` (any type). Stores `x` in `e'Object`; sets `e'Type` to `"ErrUser"`. Positional attributes (`e'Position`, `e'Traceback`) are undefined until the error is raised.
Attribute of error object `e`: the position (file/line) at which `e` was raised. Undefined if not yet raised.
Attribute of error object `e`: the stack traceback at the point `e` was raised. Undefined if not yet raised.
Attribute of error object `e`: the user-defined payload. For system errors, a string describing the error.
Attribute of error object `e`: either `"Err"` (system error) or `"ErrUser"` (user-raised error).
Statement. Raise an error whose description is the printed values of the given expressions. Useful for reporting illegal argument values.
If the Boolean expression evaluates to `true`, raise an error with the given expressions as description. Designed for precondition checking.
Assertion at level 1. If the internal `Assertions` flag ≥ 1, evaluate `bool`; if false, raise an error. Recommended for important correctness checks always active in normal mode.
Assertion at level 2. Active only when `Assertions` ≥ 2 (debug mode). For more expensive checks.
Assertion at level 3. Active only when `Assertions` ≥ 3 (extremely stringent checking).

signature: `try statements1 catch e statements2 end try;`
description: Execute `statements1`. If no error is raised, `statements2` is skipped. If an error is raised anywhere in `statements1`, execution transfers immediately to `statements2` (the remainder of `statements1` is abandoned), and the identifier `e` is bound to the raised error object. The catch block can re-raise `e` or any other error object using `error`.

signature: `for i := e1 to e2 by e3 do statements end for;`
description: Definite loop with step. Expressions must return integers `b`, `e`, `s` (begin, end, step). Loop is skipped if `s > 0` and `b > e`, or `s < 0` and `b < e`. Error if `s = 0`. Otherwise assigns `b + k·s` to `i` for `k = 0, 1, 2, ...` while `b + k·s ≤ e` (positive step) or `≥ e` (negative step).

signature: `for i := e1 to e2 do statements end for;`
description: Abbreviated form with step size 1.

signature: `for x in S do statements end for;`
description: Iterate over all elements of finite enumerated structure `S`, assigning each in turn to `x`.

signature: `for x11, ..., x1n1 in S1, ..., xm1, ..., xmnm in Sm do statements end for;`
description: Compact nested iteration over multiple structures; leftmost identifier corresponds to outermost loop.

signature: `while Boolean expression do statements end while;`
description: Check the Boolean expression; if true, execute `statements`. Repeat until the expression is false.
Execute `statements`, then check the Boolean expression. Repeat until the expression is true, then exit the loop. (Note: condition `true` exits, opposite of `while`.)
Jump to the end of the innermost enclosing loop; the termination condition is checked immediately.
In nested `for` loops, jump to the end of the loop whose variable is `identifier`; the termination condition of that loop is checked immediately.
Immediately exit the innermost enclosing loop.
In nested `for` loops, immediately exit the loop whose variable is `identifier` (allows breaking out of several loops at once).

Evaluate `expression` (must yield a string), then parse and execute that string as Magma code and return the result. The string may be either a Magma expression (no semicolon needed; result is the expression value) or a sequence of Magma statements ending in a `return` statement. The string may reference in-scope variables but cannot modify them (imported environment values are read-only).
algorithm: Dynamic parse and evaluation at runtime

description: One-line comment: all text after `//` on the same line is ignored.
Multi-line comment: all text between `/*` and `*/` is ignored.
Line continuation: the backslash and the immediately following newline are ignored, allowing a logical line to span multiple physical lines.
Return the CPU time (real number, default precision) used since the start of the Magma session. On MS-DOS, returns real (wall-clock) time instead.
Return the CPU time elapsed since time `t`. Time starts at 0.0 at session start.
Return the absolute real (wall-clock) time as a real number: seconds since 00:00:00 GMT, 1 January 1970. On MS-DOS, returns time since session start.
Return the real time elapsed since time `t`.
Return the number of CPU clock cycles since Magma's startup (matches real/wall-clock time, not process time). Returns 0 if unsupported on the current processor.
Execute `statement` and print the CPU time taken when it completes.
If the verbose flag `flag` (set via `SetVerbose`) has level ≥ 1, execute `statement` and print time taken; if level = 0, execute without printing.
As above, but activates printing when `flag` level ≥ `n`.
Return the (coarse-grained) type/category name of any object `x`.
Return the extended type/category name of any object `x`.
Given types or extended types `T` and `U`, return whether `T ISA U`, i.e., whether objects of type `T` inherit properties of type `U`. Example: `ISA(RngInt, Rng)` is `true`.
Given a string `S` naming a type, return the actual type object. Useful when an intrinsic name shadows the type symbol.
Given a structure `S`, return the type of elements of `S`. Example: `ElementType(IntegerRing())` returns `RngIntElt`.
Given structures `S` and `T`, return a covering structure `C` such that both `S` and `T` embed into `C`. Raises an error if none exists.
Given structures `S` and `T`, return whether a covering structure exists and, if so, return it.
Procedure. Reset the random number generator to initial seed `s` (0 ≤ s < 2^32) and advance to step `c` (0 ≤ c < 2^64). Equivalent to the command-line flag `-Sn` (with `c = 0`).
As above with `c = 0`.
Return the initial seed `s` and the current step `c`. Complement to `SetSeed`. Allows saving and restoring the generator state.
Return a random element of a finite set or structure `S`.
Return a random integer in the closed interval [a, b] (requires a ≤ b).
Return a random integer in [0, b] (b a non-negative integer). Calling `Random(1)` is recommended for generating random bits.
Given a string `S`, return `true` iff an intrinsic with name `S` exists in the current Magma version. If true, also return the intrinsic itself.

signature: `f := function(x1, ..., xn: parameters) statements end function;`
description: Creates a function of n ≥ 0 arguments and assigns it to `f`. At least one `return expression;` statement is required in every branch. Multiple return values are supported; the underscore `_` may be used for final undefined return slots. Optional named parameters are specified as `identifier := default_value` clauses after the colon; if omitted at call time the default is used. Inside this form, `f` cannot be used recursively (use `$$` to refer to the function itself).

signature: `function f(x1, ..., xn: parameters) statements end function;`
description: As above, but `f` is visible inside its own body, enabling direct recursion by name.

signature: `f := function(x1, ..., xn, ...: parameters) statements end function;`
description: Variadic form: accepts m ≥ n arguments. Arguments y₁…y_{n-1} bind to x₁…x_{n-1}; arguments y_n…y_m are gathered into a list `[* yn, ..., ym *]` bound to the last parameter xn.

signature: `function f(x1, ..., xn, ...: parameters) statements end function;`
description: Variadic form with self-reference by name.
Short function constructor: creates a function returning the value of a single expression. Optional parameters permitted. The name `f` is not visible inside (use `$$` for recursion).
Variadic short form of the function constructor.

signature: `p := procedure(x1, ..., xn: parameters) statements end procedure;`
description: Creates a procedure of n ≥ 0 arguments and assigns it to `p`. Reference arguments are prefixed with `~`. Inside this form, `p` cannot be referred to by name for recursion.

signature: `procedure p(x1, ..., xn: parameters) statements end procedure;`
description: As above, but `p` is visible inside its own body for direct recursive calls.

signature: `p := procedure(x1, ..., xn, ...: parameters) statements end procedure;`
description: Variadic procedure: semantics identical to variadic functions.

signature: `procedure p(x1, ..., xn, ...: parameters) statements end procedure;`
description: Variadic procedure with self-reference by name.
Short procedure constructor: `expression` must be a simple procedure call (possibly involving the arguments). Optional parameters permitted.
Variadic short form of the procedure constructor.

Forward declaration of a function or procedure `f`. Although the assignment of a value to `f` is deferred, `f` may be called from within another function or procedure defined before `f`. Must occur at the main (top) level, outside other functions or procedures.

Defines a user intrinsic named `name`. `arg-list` is a comma-separated list of typed arguments (see type specifiers above). Optional `-> ret-list` (comma-separated simple types) makes the intrinsic functional; omitting it makes it procedural. `comment-text` is documentation stored with the intrinsic (use `"` to repeat comment from preceding intrinsic). If `arg-list` ends with `...` the intrinsic is variadic. Parameters (with default values) may follow a colon in the arg-list, as in ordinary functions. Intrinsics may only be defined inside package files.
algorithm: Language construct — compiled to Magma pseudo-code on first attach; auto-recompiled when source changes.

description: (Procedure.) Attaches the package file `F`. All intrinsics within it are incorporated into Magma. If the file is subsequently modified, it is automatically recompiled before the next statement is executed — no explicit re-attach is needed. If recompilation fails, all intrinsics of the package are removed until successful recompilation.
(Procedure.) Detaches the package file `F`, removing all its intrinsics from the Magma session.

Directive placed at the top of a package file. Marks the package as *frozen*: Magma will not check whether the source has changed between statements (avoiding overhead for stable packages). The package is still recompiled when it is explicitly re-attached if needed.

Imports the identifiers in the comma-separated `ident_list` from the package file named `"filename"`. Each identifier is declared in the current scope; its value is the object assigned to the same identifier in the named file. The file must already be attached when the identifiers are used. Recommended use: sharing constants and helper functions between related package files.

If the Boolean expression `condition` is false, prints `print_args` and aborts execution with the error pointer referring to the *caller* of the intrinsic (not to the intrinsic itself). `print_args` may be any expressions involving arguments or already-defined variables.

Checks that integer argument variable `v` (which must be an argument or parameter of the enclosing intrinsic) lies in the range [L, U]. If not, prints an appropriate message and aborts with the error pointer at the caller. `L` and `U` may be any integer-valued expressions.
Checks that integer argument variable `v` satisfies v ≥ L. If not, prints an appropriate message and aborts with the error pointer at the caller. `L` may be any integer-valued expression.

(Procedure.) Attaches all package files listed in the spec file `S` (a string giving a pathname). The spec file is a tree description: files and subdirectories are listed as space-separated tokens with `{ }` grouping; a token of the form `+specfile` is recursively expanded as another spec file. All pathnames in the spec file are relative to the directory containing the spec file.
(Procedure.) Detaches all package files listed in the spec file `S`.

(Procedure.) Given a category `C` and a string `F`, appends the field name `F` to the list of valid attribute field names for structures of category `C`. For use in interactive sessions only — not inside packages. Previous fields for `C` remain valid.

Package declaration directive (not a runtime statement): given a category `C` and a comma-separated list of identifiers `F1, ..., Fn`, registers those field names as valid attribute fields for category `C`. Must be used within package files. The registration is stored with the package's compiled information and takes effect when the package is attached.
Returns the current value of attribute field `fieldname` in structure `S`. Raises a runtime error if the field is not assigned or is not valid for the category of `S`.
As `S'fieldname` but `N` is a string variable holding the field name. Useful when the field name is computed dynamically.
Returns `true` if attribute field `fieldname` in `S` currently has a value, `false` otherwise.
As above, with `N` a string holding the field name.
Assigns the value of `expression` to attribute field `fieldname` of structure `S` (discarding any previous value).
As above, with `N` a string holding the field name.
Deletes (unassigns) attribute field `fieldname` of structure `S`. The field must currently be assigned and must be a valid user-defined attribute (not a predefined system attribute).
As above, with `N` a string holding the field name.
Returns the valid attribute field names for category `C` as a sorted sequence of strings.
(Procedure.) Prints the valid attribute field names for category `C`.

Package directive (only valid inside package files): creates a new verbose flag named `F` (without quotes) with maximum allowable level `m` (a literal integer). Once declared, the flag is available throughout Magma via the standard `SetVerbose` / `GetVerbose` / `vprintf` / `vprint` mechanisms.
Declares `T` (without quotes) as a user-defined type name.

Declares `T` as a user-defined type that inherits from the user-defined types `P1, ..., Pn` (each of which must be separately declared). `ISA(T, Pi)` is true for each i; an object of type `T` will match a signature argument of type `Pi`. Note: inheriting from Magma internal types or virtual types (categories) is not currently supported.

Declares both `T` and `E` as user-defined types, and declares `E` as the *element type* of `T`: any object whose parent is of type `T` must have type `E`. This relationship is required for constructing sets and sequences with universe of type `T`.
Combination of the two previous forms: `T` and `E` are declared as user-defined types with `E` the element type of `T`, and `T` inherits from `P1, ..., Pn`.
Creates and returns an empty object of user-defined type `T`. The object has no attributes set; the caller should set relevant attributes to define the object's properties.

subsection: 2.6.3 Special Intrinsics Provided by the User
description: Required for every user-defined type `T`. Called automatically whenever an object `X` of type `T` is printed. Must be a procedure (no return value); should use `printf` without a trailing newline. Exactly one of this form or the two-argument form below must be provided.

subsection: 2.6.3 Special Intrinsics Provided by the User
signature: `intrinsic Print(X::T, L::MonStgElt) {Print X at level L} ... end intrinsic;`
description: Alternative Print intrinsic receiving a print-level string `L` ∈ `{"Default", "Minimal", "Maximal", "Magma"}`. If provided instead of the one-argument form, allows level-dependent output. Must be a procedure; use `printf` without trailing newline.

subsection: 2.6.3 Special Intrinsics Provided by the User
description: Required only when `T` is an element type (objects of type `T` have parents). Should return the parent of `X`; typically returns `X'Parent`.

subsection: 2.6.3 Special Intrinsics Provided by the User
signature: `intrinsic 'in'(e::., X::T) -> BoolElt {Return whether e is in X} ... end intrinsic;`
description: Required only when objects of type `T` have elements. Takes any object `e` and an object `X` of type `T`; returns whether `e` is an element of `X`.

subsection: 2.6.3 Special Intrinsics Provided by the User
signature: `intrinsic IsCoercible(X::T, y::.) -> BoolElt, . {Return whether y is coercible into X and the result if so} ... end intrinsic;`
description: Required when objects of type `T` have elements (so coercion `X!y` makes sense). Returns `true` and the coerced element if `y` can be coerced into `X`, or `false` and an error string otherwise. When provided, the coercion operator `X!y` automatically calls this intrinsic.
Create a character string from a sequence of keyboard characters enclosed in double quotes.
Create a binary string from the character string `s`.
Concatenate strings `s` and `t`.
Modification-concatenation: concatenate `s` and `t` in place, storing the result in `s`.
Given an enumerated sequence `s` of strings, return the concatenation of all strings in `s`.
Form the `n`-fold concatenation of string `s` (for `n ≥ 0`; `n = 0` gives the empty string).
Returns the substring of `s` consisting of the `i`-th character (as a length-1 string).
Returns the numeric value representing the `i`-th character of `s`. (Overloaded: context determines which form is used.)
Returns the sequence of characters of `s` (as length-1 strings).
Returns the sequence of numeric values representing the characters of `s`. (Overloaded for binary strings.)
Return the substring of `s` of length `k` starting at position `n`.
The length of string `s`.
Returns the position `p` (with `0 < p ≤ #s`) in string `s` at which the substring `t` first occurs, or `0` if `t` is not a substring of `s`. The empty string always returns position `1`.
Returns the code number (ASCII on most UNIX machines) of the first character of string `s`.
Returns a length-1 string corresponding to code number `n` (system-dependent; ASCII on most UNIX machines).
Returns the integer corresponding to the string of decimal digits `s`. All non-space characters must be digits (0–9) except optionally a leading `+` or `−`. Leading zeros are omitted.

Returns the integer corresponding to the string `s` of digits written in base `b`. All non-space characters must be digits less than `b` (using `A`, `B`, … for 10, 11, …) except optionally a leading `+` or `−`.
Returns the sequence of integers corresponding to the string `s` of space-separated decimal numbers. Each number may optionally begin with `+` or `−`. Leading zeros are omitted.
Convert the integer `n` into a string of decimal digits; negative `n` gives a leading `−`.
Convert integer `n` into a string of digits in base `b` (base must be in range 2–36); negative `n` gives a leading `−`.
Returns `true` if and only if strings `s` and `t` are identical (blanks are significant).
Returns `true` if and only if strings `s` and `t` are distinct (blanks are significant).
Returns `true` if and only if `s` appears as a contiguous substring of `t`. The empty string is contained in every string.
Returns `true` if and only if `s` does not appear as a contiguous substring of `t`.
Returns `true` if `s` is lexicographically less than `t` (ordering by ASCII code).
Returns `true` if `s` is lexicographically less than or equal to `t` (ordering by ASCII code).
Returns `true` if `s` is lexicographically greater than `t` (ordering by ASCII code).
Returns `true` if `s` is lexicographically greater than or equal to `t` (ordering by ASCII code).

Given string `S` and a string `D` of separator characters, return the sequence of substrings obtained by splitting `S` at any character in `D`. If `D` is omitted, `S` is split on newlines only. To split on whitespace use `" \t\n"` for `D`. An empty field is included if `S` starts with a separator; no splitting occurs if `D` is empty.

Given a regular expression string `R` and string `S`, return whether `S` matches `R`. If so, also returns the matched substring and the sequence of substrings matched by parenthesised sub-expressions (numbered left-to-right). Based on the Henry Spencer V8 regexp reimplementation; syntax and interpretation of `|`, `*`, `+`, `?`, `^`, `$`, `[]`, `\` matches UNIX `egrep`.
Print the value of the expression.
Print the values of a comma-separated list of expressions.
Print the value of the expression at the specified print level. Levels: `Default` (same as no level), `Minimal`, `Maximal`, `Magma` (produces valid Magma input where possible).
Print values of the expressions under control of the format string `format`.

Print formatted output to `file`, which must be either a filename string (opened for appending, tilde expansion performed) or a file object opened for writing. Otherwise identical to `printf`; no trailing newline is added.
If verbose flag `flag` is at level ≥ 1, print the expressions (as per `print`).
If verbose flag `flag` is at level ≥ `n`, print the expressions (as per `print`).
If verbose flag `flag` is at level ≥ 1, print using `format` (as per `printf`).
If verbose flag `flag` is at level ≥ `n`, print using `format` (as per `printf`).
Show all previous values stored in the buffer. Does not alter the buffer.
Show the `i`-th previous value stored. Does not alter the buffer.
Clear all previous values stored in the buffer.
Set the maximum size of the previous-value buffer (default: 3).
Return the current maximum size of the previous-value buffer.
Increase (push) the indentation level by 1.
Decrease (pop) the indentation level by 1. Error if the level is already 0.
Print `x` to the file named by string `F`. If the file exists, output is appended unless `Overwrite := true`, in which case the file is overwritten. Parameter: `Overwrite` (BoolElt, default `false`).
Write the binary string `s` to the file named by string `F`. If the file exists, output is appended unless `Overwrite := true`. Parameter: `Overwrite` (BoolElt, default `false`).

Print `x` in print level `L` to the file named by string `F`. `L` must be one of `"Default"`, `"Minimal"`, `"Maximal"`, or `"Magma"`. Appends unless `Overwrite := true`. Parameter: `Overwrite` (BoolElt, default `false`).
Print `x` in Magma format to the file named by string `F`. Appends unless `Overwrite := true`. Parameter: `Overwrite` (BoolElt, default `false`).
Given any Magma object `x`, return a string containing the output obtained when `x` is printed at default level.
Given a Magma object `x` and print level string `L`, return the string obtained when `x` is printed at level `L`.
Given a format string `F` and corresponding arguments (as for `printf`), return the string resulting from formatted printing of `F` and the arguments.
Redirect all Magma output to the file named by string `F`. Using `SetOutputFile(F: Overwrite := true)` empties `F` before writing. Parameter: `Overwrite` (BoolElt, default `false`).
Close the output file and direct output back to standard output.
If Magma currently has an output or log file `F`, return `true` and `F`; otherwise return `false`.

Given filename string `S` and type indicator `T`, open the file named by `S` and return a Magma file object. Tilde expansion is performed on `S`. `T` has the same interpretation as for the C function `fopen()` (e.g. `"r"` for reading, `"w"` for writing). On Windows, include `"b"` in `T` for binary mode.
Flush the buffer of file `F`.
Return the offset in bytes of the file pointer within file `F`.
Perform `fseek(F, o, p)`: move the file pointer of `F` to offset `o` relative to position `p` (0 = beginning, 1 = current, 2 = end).
Perform `rewind(F)`: move the file pointer of `F` to the beginning.
Write the characters of string `S` to file `F`.
Write the characters of string `S` followed by a newline character to file `F`.
Get and return one character from file `F` as a string. At end of file, a special EOF marker string is returned; test with `IsEof`.
Get and return one line from file `F` as a string (newline removed). At end of file, returns the EOF marker string; test with `IsEof`.
Given a string `S`, return whether `S` is the special EOF marker.
Given a length-1 string `c` and file `F`, perform `ungetc(c, F)`: push character `c` back into the input buffer of `F`.
Return the entire contents of the text file named by string `F` as a string.
Return the entire contents of the file named by string `F` as a binary string.

Given a shell command line `C` and type indicator `T`, open a pipe between the Magma process and the command. Uses the C library function `popen()`: `"r"` to read from the command's stdout, `"w"` to write to the command's stdin. Returns a File object; file I/O functions (not the pipe-specific ones below) must be used with it.

Given a shell command `C` and input string `S`, create a pipe to `C`, send `S` into its standard input, and return `C`'s standard output as a string. `S` should end with a newline if it forms a single line.

Wait for data from pipe `P` and return it as a string. Parameter: `Max` (RngIntElt, default 0 = unlimited) — if positive, at most `Max` characters are returned. Returns the EOF marker string if the pipe has been closed.

Wait for data from pipe `P` and return it as a sequence of bytes (integers in range 0–255). Parameter: `Max` (RngIntElt, default 0 = unlimited). Returns the empty sequence if the pipe has been closed.
Write the characters of string `s` to pipe `P`.
Write the bytes in byte sequence `Q` to pipe `P`. Each element of `Q` must be an integer in range 0–255.

Attempt to create a client socket connected to port `P` of host `H`. Parameters: `LocalHost` (MonStgElt, default none), `LocalPort` (RngIntElt, default 0) — the local binding values, usually left to the OS.

Range set for formal sequences: any structure supporting `in`.
Create the formal sequence of elements `x` of `F` for which `P(x)` is true. If `P(x)` is true for every element, may be abbreviated to `[! x in F !]`.
The null sequence (empty, no universe specified).
The empty sequence with universe `U`.
Given expressions `e1, …, en` evaluating to elements coercible into a single structure `U`, create the sequence `[a1, a2, …, an]`. The expression `x^^n` repeats `x` n times.

Sequence of values `e(x)` for those `x ∈ E` with `P(x)` true. Abbreviated to `[ e(x) : x in E ]` when `P` is always true.

signature: `[ U | e(x) : x in E | P(x) ]`
description: As above, coerced into universe `U`.
Sequence of values `e(x1,…,xk)` for tuples satisfying the predicate. Successive identical ranges may be abbreviated `xi, xi+1 in Ei`; predicate may be omitted if always true.
As above, with all values coerced into `U`.
Enumerated sequence of integers `i, i+1, …, j`. If `j < i`, returns the empty sequence. `U`, if specified, must be the ring of integers.

Given literal integers `m1, …, mn`, build the enumerated sequence `[m1, …, mn]` in a time- and space-efficient way.

Returns the structure comprising all enumerated sequences of elements of structure `R`. If `R` is itself a sequence or set, returns the power structure of its universe. Permitted operations on power sequences: printing, membership testing (`in`), and coercion (`!`).
Returns `true` if enumerated sequence `S` is an element of the power sequence `P` (i.e. all elements of `S` are in or coercible into the base structure `R`); `false` otherwise.
Return a sequence with universe `R` consisting of the entries of enumerated sequence `S`, coerced into `R`. Error if any element cannot be coerced.
The length of enumerated sequence `S` — the index of the last defined term. Length of the empty sequence is zero.
The parent structure of sequence `S` — the power sequence over the universe of `S`.
The common structure (universe) to which all elements of `S` belong. Error if `S` is the null sequence.

The `i`-th term of sequence `S`. Error if `i ≤ 0`, or `i > #S + 1`, or `S[i]` is undefined. `i` may be a multi-index. Also valid as the left-hand side of an assignment `S[i] := x`; assigning beyond `#S` extends the sequence (with undefined intermediate terms).
Subsequence `[S[i1], …, S[ir]]` selected by the integer sequence `I`. Error if any term of `I` is out of range. Unlike `[ S[i] : i in I ]`, undefined entries in range are copied (not an error).
For a non-empty complete sequence `S` with `lt` and `eq` defined on its universe: returns the minimal element `s` and the first position `i` with `s = S[i]`.
For a non-empty complete sequence `S` with `gt` and `eq` defined: returns the maximal element and its first position.

signature: `Index(S, x)` / `Index(S, x, f)` / `Position(S, x)` / `Position(S, x, f)`
description: Position of the first occurrence of `x` in `S`, or zero if not present. The two-argument form `f` starts the search at position `f`, saving time on repeated searches.
An arbitrary element chosen from enumerated sequence `R`.
A uniformly random element chosen from enumerated sequence `R`. Successive calls return independently chosen elements. Error if `R` is empty.
For sequence `R` of length `r`, returns the `r` entries as separate return values (in order).
Returns the enumerated sequence `R` itself (included for completeness/uniformity).
Add `x` to the end of `S`, giving `[s1, …, sn, x]`.
Remove the first occurrence of `x` from `S`; if `x` is not in `S`, `S` is unchanged.
Add `x` to the end of `S` only if no term of `S` equals `x`; otherwise `S` is unchanged.
Insert `x` at position `i`, shifting `S[i], …, S[n]` down one place. If `i > n`, the new length is `i` and intermediate terms are undefined.

signature: `Insert(~S, k, m, T)` / `Insert(S, k, m, T)`
description: Replace terms `S[k], …, S[m]` with the terms of `T`, giving `[s1, …, sk-1, t1, …, tl, sm+1, …, sn]`. Error if `k ≤ 0` or `k > m+1`. If `T` is empty, terms `sk, …, sm` are deleted.
Remove the last term of `S`, giving `[s1, …, sn-1]`. Error if `S` is empty.
Remove the `i`-th term from `S`. Error if `i < 1` or `i > n`.
Reverse the order of terms in the complete sequence `S`, giving `[sn, …, s1]`.
Cyclically rotate complete sequence `S` by `p` positions: positive `p` rotates right, negative `p` rotates `|p|` positions left, zero does nothing.
Sort complete sequence `S` into increasing order using quicksort, requiring `lt` and `eq` on the universe.
Sort `S` using comparison function `C(x, y)` returning negative/zero/positive. The three-return-value procedure form also sets the permutation `p` applied to `S`.
Sort `S` in place and simultaneously apply the same transpositions to `T`.
Make the `i`-th term of `S` undefined. `i` may exceed `#S`; `i ≤ 0` produces an error.
Coerce all elements of `S` into structure `V` (which must contain the current universe `U`). Procedure form modifies in place; function form returns the new sequence.
Attempt to coerce all elements of `S` into `V`; returns `true` and the new sequence on success, `false` otherwise.

description: Concatenation of `S` and `T`, giving `[s1, …, sn, t1, …, tm]`. A common over-structure is sought if universes differ; error if none exists.

description: Mutation assignment: replaces `S` with `S cat T`.

description: For complete non-empty `S` and sequence of positive integers `P` with sum `#S`: sequence of sub-sequences of lengths `P[1], P[2], …`.

description: Given a set `S`, construct a sequence whose terms are the elements of `S` in some arbitrary order.

description: Given a sequence `S`, create a set whose elements are the distinct terms of `S`.
Pointwise logical `and` of `S` and `T`. Reference form stores result in `S`.
Pointwise logical `or` of `S` and `T`. Reference form stores result in `S`.
Pointwise logical `xor` of `S` and `T`. Reference form stores result in `S`.
Pointwise logical `not` of `S`. Reference form stores result in `S`.
Returns `true` iff every term `S[i]` for `1 ≤ i ≤ #S` is defined.
Returns `true` iff `S[i]` is defined. Returns `false` if `i > #S`; error if `i < 1`. Supports multi-indices.
Returns `true` iff enumerated sequence `S` is empty.
Returns `true` iff `S` is empty and its universe is undefined (the null sequence).
Returns `true` if `x` occurs as a term of enumerated or formal sequence `S`. Coercion is attempted if `x` is not in the universe; error if coercion fails.
Returns `true` if `x` does not occur as a term of `S`. Same coercion behaviour.

Returns `true` if `S` appears as a subsequence of `T`. Default `Kind := "Consecutive"` (consecutive elements); `"Sequential"` (in order, not necessarily consecutive); `"Setwise"` (set containment). Coercion is attempted if universes differ.
Returns `true` if sequences `S` and `T` are equal. Coercion attempted if universes differ.
Returns `true` if `S` and `T` are not equal.
`true` iff `S` strictly precedes `T` in lexicographic order: `S[k] < T[k]` at the first difference, or `S` is a proper prefix of `T`.
`true` iff `S lt T` or `S eq T`.
`true` iff `S gt T` or `S eq T`.
`true` iff `S` strictly follows `T`: `S[k] > T[k]` at the first difference, or `T` is a proper prefix of `S`.
Inside a sequence constructor, refers to the already-computed entry `s[n]` of the sequence under construction, or the sequence itself. Allows recursive sequence definitions.

For a complete sequence `S = [a1, …, an]` and associative operator `◦`, computes `a1 ◦ a2 ◦ … ◦ an`. Supported operators: `+`, `*`, `and`, `or`, `join`, `meet`, `cat`. For a single-element sequence returns that element. For empty sequences with universe: `&+` → `0`, `&*` → `1`, `&and` → `true`, `&or` → `false`, `&join` → empty, `&cat` → empty; `&meet` → error. For the null sequence: `&and` and `&or` return `true`/`false`; all others error.

signature: `for x in S do statements; end for;`
description: Iterate over the defined terms of enumerated sequence `S`. Undefined terms are skipped. When multiple range sequences are used in a constructor, the first range forms the innermost loop (last-varying variable).
Given a list of sets or algebraic structures R1, …, Rk, construct the cartesian product set R1 × ··· × Rk.
Given structures R and S, construct the cartesian product R × S. Equivalent to calling the `car` constructor with two arguments.
Given a sequence or tuple L of structures, construct the cartesian product of the elements of L.
Given a structure R and a non-negative integer k, construct the cartesian power set Rk.

Given a cartesian product C whose factors may themselves be cartesian products, return the cartesian product of the base (non-cartesian-product) structures considered in depth-first order. See also `Flat` for the element version.
Return the number of components (factors) of the cartesian product C.
Return the i-th component (factor) of the cartesian product C.
Return the cardinality of the cartesian product C.
Return a representative element of the cartesian product C.
Return a random element of the cartesian product C.
Given a cartesian product C = R1 × ··· × Rk and elements a1, …, ak with ai ∈ Ri, create the tuple T = ⟨a1, a2, …, ak⟩ of C.
Given elements a1, …, ak with ai ∈ Ri, create the tuple T = ⟨a1, …, ak⟩. If the corresponding cartesian product C does not already exist it is created at evaluation time.
Return the tuple formed by adding object x to the end of tuple T. The result lies in a new cartesian product.
(Procedure.) Destructively add object x to the end of tuple T. The new T lies in a new cartesian product.
Return the tuple formed by removing the last term of tuple T. The length of T must be greater than 1. The result lies in a new cartesian product.
(Procedure.) Destructively remove the last term of tuple T. The length of T must be greater than 1. The new T lies in a new cartesian product.
Construct the flattened version of tuple T, performing the flattening depth-first (analogous to `Flat` for cartesian products).
Return the cartesian product to which the tuple T belongs.
Return the number of components of the tuple T.
Return the i-th component of the tuple T. This indexing may also be used on the left-hand side to modify T in place.
Given a tuple T of length n, return the n entries of T in order (as multiple return values).
Given a tuple T, return a list (sequence) containing the entries of T.
Return `true` if and only if tuples T and U are equal.
Return `true` if and only if tuples T and U are distinct.
For a tuple T whose components all lie in a structure supporting multiplication and with a common over-structure, return the product of all entries.
The empty list.
Given expressions e1, …, en defining elements a1, a2, …, an, create the list containing a1, a2, …, an.
The list formed by concatenating the terms of S with the terms of T, i.e. `[* s1, …, sn, t1, …, tm *]`.
(Procedure.) Destructively concatenate the terms of T to S; S becomes `[* s1, …, sn, t1, …, tm *]`.
The list formed by adding the object x to the end of S, i.e. `[* s1, …, sn, x *]`.
(Procedure.) Destructively add the object x to the end of S; S becomes `[* s1, …, sn, x *]`.

Create the list formed by inserting x at position i in S and moving S[i], …, S[n] down one place, i.e. `[* s1, …, s_{i−1}, x, si, …, sn *]`. i must not exceed n + 1. The procedural form (reference `~S`) replaces S in place and is much more efficient since S is not copied; the functional form returns the new list.
The list formed by removing the last term of S, i.e. `[* s1, …, s_{n−1} *]`.
(Procedure.) Destructively remove the last term of S; S becomes `[* s1, …, s_{n−1} *]`.
Given a sequence Q, construct a list whose terms are the elements of Q taken in the same order.
Given a tuple T, construct a list whose terms are the elements of T taken in the same order.
Given a list L, return the same list in reverse order.
The length of the list S.
Return whether S is empty (has zero length).
Return the i-th term of the list S. An error results if i ≤ 0 or i > #S + 1. i is allowed to be a multi-index (see Section 8.3.1).
Return the sublist of S given by the indices in the sequence I. Each index in I must be in the range [1..l], where l is the length of S.
Checks whether the i-th item in L is defined; returns true if i ≤ #L and false otherwise.
Redefine the i-th term of the list S to be x. If i ≤ 0, an error results. If i = #S + 1, x is appended to S. If i > #S + 1, an error results. i is allowed to be a multi-index.
Create the null associative array with no index universe. The first assignment to the array determines its index universe.
Create the empty associative array with index universe `I`.

Set the value in `A` associated with index `x` to `y`. If `x` is not coercible into the current index universe `I` of `A`, an attempt is first made to lift the index universe of `A` to contain both `I` and `x`.
Given an index `x` coercible into the index universe `I` of `A`, return the value associated with `x`. Raises an error if `x` is not among the current keys of `A`.
Given an index `x` coercible into the index universe `I` of `A`, return whether `x` is currently in the keys of `A`; if so, also return the value `A[x]`.
(Procedure.) Destructively remove the value indexed by `x` from array `A`. If `x` is not present as an index, nothing happens (no error is raised).
Return the index universe `I` of associative array `A`, in which the current keys lie.
Return the current keys of `A` as a set. Constructs a new copy of the key set; not intended as a fast accessor — call only when the full set is needed.
Given a list of two or more structures S1, S2, ..., Sk, creates and returns their coproduct C together with a sequence of injection maps [m1, m2, ..., mk] where mi : Si → C.
As above but accepts a sequence (rather than an explicit list) of constituent structures. Useful for parameterised families. Returns C and the sequence of injection maps.
Given a coproduct injection map m and an element e of the corresponding constituent, returns the coproduct element version of e.
Given a coproduct C and an element e of one of the constituents of C whose type is unique within C, returns the coproduct element version of e.
Given a coproduct C, returns the sequence of injection maps (the same sequence returned as the second argument from the `cop<>` constructor).
Given a coproduct C, returns the number of constituents of C.
Given a coproduct C and an integer i between 1 and the length of C, returns the i-th constituent structure of C.
Given an element x from a coproduct C, returns the constituent number (index) of C to which x belongs.
Given an element x of some coproduct C, returns x as an element of the structure that formed its parent before it was mapped into C.
Given a coproduct C whose constituents may themselves be coproducts, returns the coproduct of the base structures considered in depth-first order.
Given maps n1, ..., nm from structures S1, ..., Sm that compose the coproduct C to some structure S, returns the universal map C → S.

Construct the record format corresponding to the non-empty fieldname list `L`. Each term of `L` must be one of: (a) `fieldname` — no restriction on values; (b) `fieldname : expression` — expression evaluates to a magma that is the required parent; or (c) `fieldname : expression` — expression evaluates to a category that is the required category. Fieldnames must consist of characters that form a valid identifier name (not a string).

Given a record format `F`, construct the record corresponding to the field assignment list `L`. Each term of `L` must have the form `fieldname := expression`, where `fieldname` is declared in `F` and the value of the expression conforms (directly or by coercion) to any restriction on that field. `L` may be empty and the fieldnames may appear in any order.
The record format of record `r`.
The fieldnames of record format `F`, returned as a sequence of strings.
The fieldnames of record `r`, returned as a sequence of strings.
Return the value of the field named `fieldname` in record `r`. The format of `r` must include this fieldname and the field must currently be assigned.

Assign (or reassign) the field named `fieldname` in record `r` to the value of `expression`. The format of `r` must include this fieldname, and the value must satisfy (directly or by coercion) any restriction on the field.
(Statement.) Delete the current value of the field named `fieldname` in record `r`.
Returns `true` if and only if the field named `fieldname` in record `r` currently holds a value.

Given an expression `s` that evaluates to a string, return the field of record `r` whose fieldname corresponds to that string. The format of `r` must include this fieldname and the field must be assigned. Given a finite structure A, a structure B, and a full graph G of A × B (set, sequence, or list of tuples or arrow-pairs), construct the mapping f : A → B. Every element of A must appear exactly once as a first component.

Return whether the preimage of x under f can be taken, and the preimage as a second return value if it can.
The parent of m.

The codomain of the maps for which P is the parent.

description: Given a univariate polynomial f over ring R, returns the factorization as a sequence of (irreducible factor, multiplicity) pairs (each factor is normalized), plus the unit u such that f = u · ∏ qᵢ^kᵢ. R must be: a finite field F_q, Z, Q, an algebraic number field Q(α), a local ring, a polynomial ring, function field, or finite-dimensional affine algebra over any of the above. Parameter `Al` (MonStgElt, default `"Default"`): selects the factorization algorithm over finite fields. Values: `"Default"` (automatic), `"BerlekampSmall"` or `"BerlekampLarge"` (Berlekamp variants), `"GKS"` (von zur Gathen/Kaltofen/Shoup).
algorithm: Over small finite fields: Berlekamp algorithm **[Knu97 §4.6.2]** / **[vzGG99 §14.8]** (fast linear algebra). Over medium/large finite fields: von zur Gathen/Kaltofen/Shoup algorithm **[vzGS92, KS95, Sho95]**. Over Z or Q (since V2.8): van Hoeij's algorithm **[vH02, vH01]** — factorize mod a small prime, Hensel-lift using Shoup's tree-lifting **[vzGG99 §15.5]**, then find correct combinations via a Knapsack problem solved by LLL lattice-basis reduction **[LLL82]** (not by exhaustive search as in Berlekamp–Zassenhaus). Over algebraic number fields, algebraic function fields, and affine algebras: Trager's norm-based algorithm **[Tra76]** (substitution + resultant to reduce variable count; then van Hoeij combination in characteristic 0). Over function fields in small characteristic with inseparable extensions: algorithm of Allan Steel **[Ste05]**.

description: Given sparse m × n integer matrix `A` (over **Z**) and a positive integer `M` (or its factorisation sequence `L`): compute a vector `v` such that v·A^T ≡ 0 (mod M); `v` is non-zero with high probability. Parameter `Lanczos` (default `false`): if `true`, use the Lanczos algorithm instead of the default. **Memory guidance:** 100,000 × 100,000 systems require ~500 MB; 200,000 × 200,000 require ~1.5–2.0 GB.

description: (Procedure.) Simplify the algebraically closed field `A` in place so that the affine algebra representing it is a true field (i.e. the multivariate polynomial ideal of defining polynomials is maximal). First performs a partial simplification by calling `MinimalPolynomial` on all variables and on all sums of two variables of `A` (forcing the corresponding minimal polynomials to be irreducible, causing many simplifications). Then performs all remaining simplifications by successively computing absolute representations and factorising the absolute polynomials that arise. This final step can be very expensive if the absolute degree exceeds about 20. Parameter `Partial` (boolean, default `false`): if `true`, perform only the partial simplification (usually fast and often sufficient).
algorithm: Partial step: `MinimalPolynomial`-based splitting **[Ste02, Ste10]**. Full step: successive absolute field computation and factorisation.

Returns the i-th indeterminate of the function field F as an element of F.

Parameters: `Ramification` (BoolElt, default false) — pre-compute inertia groups at all ramified primes and conductors of all representations; `FactorDiscriminant` (BoolElt or tuple, default false) — whether to fully factorise the discriminant of f to determine which primes ramify (incomplete factorisation causes Magma to assume unramified primes in the unfactored part, and to print "(?)" after conductor values); `p0` (RngIntElt, default auto) — which p-adic field to use for roots of f, must be chosen so that `GaloisGroup(f: Prime := p0)` succeeds.
Given the normal closure F of K/Q, convert an abstract group character of Gal(F/Q), or a sequence of its trace values, into an Artin representation.

Construct the permutation representation A of the absolute Galois group of Q on the embeddings of K into C. A has dimension [K : Q] and equals the permutation representation of Gal(F/Q) on the cosets of Gal(F/K), where F is the normal closure of K.
Construct the determinant of a given Artin representation. The result is a 1-dimensional Artin representation attached to the same field.

Given an Artin representation A (attached to some number field) known to factor through the Galois closure of K, attempt to recognise it as such. Returns the resulting Artin representation attached to K and true if successful, or 0 and false if it proves no such representation exists. Parameter: `MinPrimes` (RngIntElt, default 20) — number of additional primes for which to compare traces of Frobenius elements.

Conductor of an Artin representation A (A must be a true representation, i.e. its character is not a generalised character). Computes all necessary local information if Artin representations were defined with `Ramification := false`; the first call may therefore take some time.
Decompose an Artin representation A into irreducible constituents. Returns a sequence of tuples `[...<Aᵢ, nᵢ>...]` with Aᵢ irreducible and nᵢ its exponent in A (nonzero but possibly negative).
Returns the polynomial whose roots `Group(A)` permutes.

description: Returns a sequence of partial Puiseux series expansions of the roots of `f` over a series ring. Roots are returned with relative precision at least n/d, where d is the lcm of the exponent denominator of the expansion and the exponent denominators of the coefficients of `f`. With `n = 0`, returns expansions from the Newton polygon stage only. Parameters: `PreciseRoot` (`BoolElt`, default `false`) — checks if any partial expansion is an exact root and returns it with full precision; `TestSquarefree` (`BoolElt`, default `true`) — remove multiple factors before expanding (set to `false` to avoid precision loss when f is known squarefree); `NoExtensions` (`BoolElt`, default `false`) — find expansions in the original Puiseux ring only without field extensions; `LowerFaces` (`BoolElt`, default `true`) — if `false`, expansions with negative valuations are not found; `OneRoot` (`BoolElt`, default `false`) — return only representatives of conjugate roots rather than all roots.
algorithm: Walker's algorithm **[Wal78]**. May not terminate for char k ≤ deg f (see **[Gri95]**, pp. 269–272).

Define a power series root of a polynomial `p` using initial expansion `ip` and exponent lattice `(1/e)L`. The defining polynomial `p` is `dp` when optional parameter `subs` (default `[]`) is empty, or obtained by substituting the elements of `subs` into the variables of `dp`. The initial expansion must be sufficiently long to uniquely identify a root (see **[Bec07, Cond. 4.3]**). In expansions, variables represent `e`-th roots, so `x₁ x₂²` is really `x₁^{1/e} x₂^{2/e}`. Simpler overloads omit `L` (assuming the standard integral lattice) or `e` (assuming `e = 1`). No strong correctness checks are performed at construction time; incorrect initial data is only revealed during later expansion.

Given a series `s`, a sequence `nu` of vectors in the dual of its exponent lattice, and a sequence `v` (same length) of power series in a common domain with compatible coefficient field: returns the series obtained by substituting `x^μ ↦ ∏ᵢ v[i]^⟨nu[i],μ⟩`. Requires `nu` and `v` to fulfill a convergence condition (see **[Bec07, Cond. 4.6]**).

The unique series with zero constant term defined by a polynomial `p ∈ k[x₁,…,xₙ][z]` or `k[[x₁,…,xₙ]][z]` fulfilling the implicit function theorem conditions: `p(0,…,0) = 0` and `∂p/∂z(0,…,0) ≠ 0`. `dp` may be substituted with the series in optional parameter `subs` (default `[]`). `dp` should have coefficients in a multivariate polynomial ring.

Assumes `p` is a univariate polynomial over a multivariate polynomial ring `S = k[x₁,…,xᵣ]` and that `p` is quasi-ordinary (the user must ensure this for efficiency). Returns: (1) the exponent lattice `⟨Γ₀, e₀⟩` of the input polynomial; (2) a complete list of rational parametrizations in format `⟨λ, s, N, E⟩` where `λ` is a sequence of `r` field elements, `s` is a fractionary algebraic power series of type `RngPowAlgElt` solving the scaled polynomial, `N` is the index of `e₀⁻¹Γ₀` in the exponent lattice of `s`, and `E` is the degree of the coefficient field extension needed. Optional parameter `Gamma` (lattice, default `StandardLattice`) specifies Γ₀. Parameter `subs` (default `[]`): a sequence of `r` power series in a common domain — when provided, variables in `p` are substituted by the corresponding series and the resulting polynomial must be quasi-ordinary; `Gamma` has no effect in this case. Parameter `Duval` (BoolElt, default `false`): if `false`, returns a complete set of representatives (up to conjugacy) of Puiseux series roots with λ-vectors always vectors of ones; if `true`, applies Duval's trick, requiring automorphisms of `k[[x₁,…,xₙ]]` in advance but avoiding field extensions. Parameter `OnlySingular` (BoolElt, default `false`): if `true`, returns only parametrizations corresponding to singular branches. Parameters `ExtName` (MonStgElt, default `"gamma"`) and `ExtCount` (RngIntElt, default `0`) control naming of algebraic elements when the ground field must be extended; the last return value is `ExtCount` plus the number of field extensions introduced.
algorithm: Newton–Puiseux algorithm with Duval's extension **[Bec07, Sec. 4.3]**

description: For a finitely generated subgroup G of GL(n, K): constructs a congruence homomorphism from G into GL(n, Fq) for some prime power q. Returns the congruence image H, the homomorphism, and the list of images of generators of G. The kernel N is the normal subgroup of G whose torsion elements are all unipotent (torsion-free when char K = 0). Parameters: `Virtual` (BoolElt, default `false`) — if true, the homomorphism satisfies additional properties from **[DFO11]** enabling the virtual-property tests of §61.4; `Prime` (RngIntElt, default `3`) — when char K = 0 and positive, a lower bound for the characteristic of the congruence image; if 0, constructs an image over a characteristic-0 field; `Limit` (RngIntElt, default `10`) — for groups over rational function fields, limits the degree of field extensions (char K > 0) or the modulus tuples examined (char K = 0); `ExtDegree` (RngIntElt, default `1`) — for algebraic function fields of positive characteristic, the minimum degree of the coefficient field extension.

For a finitely generated subgroup G of GL(n, K): returns `true` if G is finite, otherwise `false`. Parameters: `NumberRandom` (RngIntElt, default `10`) — number of random elements tested for finite order first; `Presentation` (MonStgElt, default `"CT"`) — how the presentation for the congruence image is constructed: `"CT"` uses `CompositionTreeVerify`, `"PC"` uses `LMGSolubleRadical` (when image is soluble), `"FP"` uses `FPGroup` or `FPGroupStrong`; `Small` (RngIntElt, default `10⁵`) — if image order is below this, use `FPGroup`; `OrderLimit` (RngIntElt, default `10¹²`) — if image order is below this (and above `Small`), use `FPGroupStrong`; `Algebra` (BoolElt, default `true`) — if true and K is a function field, uses the "algebra algorithm" of **[DF09]** (char 0) or **[DFO09]** (char > 0); `Nilpotent` (BoolElt, default `false`) — if true, calls a special procedure for nilpotent groups **[DF08, Section 4.3]**; `UseCongruence` (BoolElt, default `false`) — for K = Q or a number field, forces use of congruence homomorphism machinery; `DetermineOrder` (BoolElt, default `false`) — if true and G is finite, also returns the order of G; `Prime` (RngIntElt, default `3`) — same meaning as in `CongruenceImage`.
algorithm: Composite: algebra algorithm **[DF09]** / **[DFO09]** or congruence-homomorphism + presentation evaluation **[DFO12, DF09, DFO09, DF08]**.

description: Input is a finite subgroup G of GL(n, K). If successful, returns `true` and an isomorphic copy of G in GL(n, Fq) for some prime power q; otherwise returns `false`. Assuming `A` is the basic algebra of p-group G and `B` that of a subgroup, returns the change-of-basis matrix making the standard free A-module into a direct sum of standard free B-modules, its inverse, and a set of coset representatives of PCGroup(B) in PCGroup(A).
Takes compact resolution PR for the trivial G-module and restriction data RD for a subgroup H, returns the restriction of the resolution to a complex of H-modules.

Computes the images of the generators of the cohomology ring of G under restriction to a subgroup H. Inputs: resolutions and cohomology generators for G (PR1, AC1) and H (PR2, AC2) and cohomology relations for H (REL2).
Returns the images of generators of the cohomology ring of a quotient Q in the cohomology ring of G. Input θ : G → Q is the quotient map; PR1, AC1 for G; PR2, AC2 for Q; REL1 for G.

description: Constructs a null homotopy H of the null-homotopic chain map f (so that f = dH − Hd). Throws an error if f is not null-homotopic.

description: Confirms that H is a null homotopy of f, i.e. that f = dH − Hd.

Creates the quaternion algebra A over field K with generators i, j satisfying i² = a, j² = b, ji = −ij (char ≠ 2) or ji = (i+1)j (char 2). The third generator is k = ij. K may be any Magma field type.
Given a quaternion algebra A and a sequence S of 3 strings, assigns the strings as names for the generators (basis elements other than 1). Called automatically by the bracket constructor `< >`.

Given a positive squarefree integer N, returns a rational quaternion algebra of discriminant N. Parameters: `Al` (`"TraceValues"` default for odd number of prime factors, computes a basis also spanning a maximal order; `"Random"` uses a faster probabilistic algorithm); `Optimized` (default `true`).
algorithm: For odd-prime-factor count: trace-value algorithm yielding a maximal-order basis. Probabilistic variant otherwise.

description: Given a squarefree polynomial N ∈ F_q[x] for odd q, returns a quaternion algebra over F_q(x) of discriminant N.

Given an ideal I of a number field F with an even number of prime ideal factors, returns the quaternion algebra over F ramified exactly at the primes dividing I (uses radical of I). Parameter: `Optimized` (default `true`).

Given an ideal I and a subset S of real places of F such that #prime-factors-of-I ≡ #S (mod 2), returns the algebra ramified exactly at primes dividing I and at real places in S. Parameter: `Optimized` (default `true`).
Given an even set S of non-complex places of a number field F, returns the quaternion algebra ramified exactly at S. Parameter: `Optimized` (default `true`).

Creates the rational quaternion algebra Q⟨i, j⟩ where Z[i] and Z[j] are quadratic suborders of discriminants D1 and D2, and Z[ij − ji] has discriminant D1·D2 − T². D1·D2 and T must have the same parity; each of D1, D2, D1D2 − T² must be a discriminant of a quadratic order (non-square integer ≡ 0 or 1 mod 4). The algebra is not always in standard form.
algorithm: Structure determined by discriminants of three quadratic subfields.

description: Given S a sequence of elements in a quaternion algebra over Q or F_q(X), returns the order generated by S over Z or F_q[X]. Raises an error if S does not generate an order. Parameter: `IsBasis` (default `false`; if `true`, uses S directly as a basis).
Given a ring R and a sequence S of 4 elements of a quaternion algebra over Q or F_q(X), returns the R-order with basis S. Parameter: `Check` (default `true`).
Constructs a maximal order in quaternion algebra A over a number field, Q, F_q(X) with q odd, or the field of fractions of a number ring.
algorithm: Over F_q(X): standard Round-2 algorithm **[Fri97, IR93]**. Over Q or number fields: a quaternion-optimised variant — factorise discriminant of a tame order, then for each prime p compute a p-maximal order; see Algorithm 4.3.8 in **[Voi05]** and **[Voi11]**.

description: For O a quaternion order over Z, F_q[X] (q odd) or a number ring, returns a maximal order containing O.
For O a quaternion order and prime (ideal) p, returns a p-maximal order O′ containing O. Returns the p-adic valuation of disc(O′) (0 or 1) as a second value.

Returns an order O whose odd reduced discriminant is squarefree. Ignores even primes and does not test remaining odd primes for maximality. A must be over a number field or field of fractions of a number ring.

description: Given a maximal quaternion order O over a number ring and N, returns an Eichler order of level N inside O.

description: Constructs the quaternion order Z⟨x, y⟩ where Z[x] and Z[y] are quadratic subrings of discriminants D1 and D2, and Z[xy − yx] has discriminant D1·D2 − T². Container algebra is generally not in standard form.
algorithm: Structure from discriminants of quadratic subrings.

description: The zero element of the quaternion algebra A.
The identity element of A.
For 1 ≤ i ≤ 3, returns the i-th generator of A as an algebra over its base ring. (Element 1 is always the first basis element, never returned as a generating element.)
Coerces x into A; x may be an algebra element, module element, sequence, order element, or something coercible into the coefficient ring.
Sum of x and y.
Difference of x and y.
Product of x and y.

True iff x and y are equal.
True iff x and y are not equal.

True iff x is not in the algebra A.

Sequence of coordinates of x in terms of the basis of its parent.

The reduced discriminant of A over Q, F_q(X) or a number field. Over Q or F_q(X): product of ramified primes. Over number fields: product of ramified prime ideals plus sequence of ramified infinite places.
Returns integers a, b in the base field F such that i² = a, j² = b, ji = −ij; also returns the standard quaternion algebra B = QuaternionAlgebra<F|a,b> and the isomorphism A → B.

description: True iff the prime or prime ideal p is ramified (resp. unramified) in A.

For A (over Q, a number field, or F_q(x) with q odd) and prime (ideal) p unramified in A: returns the matrix ring over the completion F_p, a map A → M₂(F_p), and the embedding F → F_p. For a p-maximal order O, the map restricts to O → M₂(R_p). Parameter: `Precision`.

For A over Q, F_q(X) or a number field F, and K a quadratic extension of F: true iff an embedding K → A over F exists (checked by comparison of ramified places, see **[Vig80, Cor. III.3.5]**). Second return: a witness place if no embedding; if embedding exists and `ComputeEmbedding := true`, also returns the result of `Embed`. Parameter: `ComputeEmbedding` (default `false`).

For K a quadratic extension of the base field F of A: returns an embedding K → A over F as an element of A (image of primitive generator of K) and the map K → A. Parameter: `Al` (`"NormEquation"` default, solves a relative norm equation; `"Search"` uses naive search).

description: For Oc a quadratic order over base number ring R and O a quaternion order over R: computes an embedding Oc → O, returning the image of the second generator Oc.2 and the embedding map Oc → O. Parameter: `Al` (`"NormEquation"` default or `"Search"`).
True iff A over a number field, Q, or F_q(X) with q odd is (totally) definite.
True iff A is indefinite.

True iff the quaternion algebra A with base field F ∈ {Q, F_q(X), number field} is isomorphic to M₂(F), i.e. has no ramified places. If `Isomorphism := true` (default `false`) and A ≅ M₂(F), also returns M₂(F) and the isomorphism A → M₂(F).

True iff the associative algebra B is a quaternion algebra. If true, returns the associated quaternion algebra A in standard form and an algebra homomorphism B → A.

Factorisation of the reduced discriminant of S.

True iff the completion of O at prime (ideal) p is Gorenstein.
Intersection of quaternion orders O1 and O2.

Right ideal of order S generated by sequence X.
Two-sided ideal of order S generated by sequence X.

The right order of ideal I (elements mapping I to itself under right multiplication).

Representatives for the left or right locally free ideal classes of S (Eichler or maximal order over Q, F_q(X), or a number field). For definite algebras: `Support` parameter specifies a sequence of primes generating the narrow class group that do not ramify in A. For indefinite algebras: representatives obtained from a ray class group of the base field.

Two-sided ideal class group of S as an abstract abelian group, plus a map from the group to the set of two-sided ideal classes. Inverses computable efficiently (enabling discrete logarithms). S must be Eichler or maximal. `Support` parameter as above.

For a maximal order (or Eichler order of level N) in A: representatives for conjugacy classes of maximal orders (resp. orders of level N) in A. For definite algebras: equivalent to computing right ideal classes.

The conjugate ideal of I.

For a quaternion algebra A over any field F not of characteristic 2: returns the underlying F-space with the norm form as inner product, plus a map A → structure.

Gram matrix of the quaternion order S or ideal I over Z or F_q[X] w.r.t. the norm on the basis.

A basis B for the definite quaternion order or ideal S, together with its Gram matrix G. The Gram matrix G is unique; the basis B is not.

"Reduced" basis for order O or ideal I over a number ring. Definite algebra: LLL-reduced w.r.t. the norm form. Indefinite algebra: reduced w.r.t. a Minkowski-like embedding, see **[KV10, Section 4]**.

For a quaternion algebra A over Q or a number field F: returns A′ = ((a,b)/F) with a, b small, and an isomorphism A → A′.
Sequence of all elements x (up to sign) in the definite quaternion order O or ideal I over Z with reduced norm in [A, …, B] (or [0, …, B] if only B given).
Elements x (up to sign) in the definite quaternion order O or ideal I over a number ring with absolute trace of norm in [A, …, B] (or [0, …, B]).

description: For orders S, T over Q, F_q(X) (q odd) or a number field: true iff S and T are isomorphic. Indefinite case currently requires S, T to be maximal.
