description: For a tableau monoid `M` and a word `w` from its ordered monoid: the tableau corresponding to `w` through row insertion.
For a tableau monoid `M` and an element `u` of the associated plactic monoid: the tableau corresponding to `u` through row insertion.
For `M` over the positive integers: the tableau corresponding to the word `i₁ * ⋯ * i_n`.

For `M` over the positive integers and a sequence `Q` of sequences of non-negative integers: the tableau with the elements of `Q` as its rows (zeroes indicate skew entries). Must satisfy the row/column conditions.
For a tableau monoid `M` and a sequence `Q` of words from its ordered monoid: the (non-skew) tableau with the words of `Q` as rows.
The set of all standard tableaux from tableau monoid `M` of shape `P` (a partition). If `M` is given it must contain more than `Weight(P)` labels.
The set of all standard tableaux from `M` of weight `n` (positive integer). If `M` is given it must contain at least `n` labels.
The set of all tableaux of shape `S` (a partition) using only the first `m` labels of `M`. If `M` is given it must contain at least `m` labels.

The set of all tableaux from `M` having shape `S` (a partition) and content `C` (non-negative integers; see §145.4.6). If `C` prescribes fewer cells than fill `S`, the tableau within the given shape is returned. If `M` is given it must have at least as many labels as `C` has entries.
The set of all tableaux from `M` with content `C` (non-negative integers; see §145.4.6). If `M` is given it must have at least as many labels as `C` has entries.

For a Young diagram given by partition `P` or tableau `t`, and `(i, j)` on the shape: perform a random hook walk starting at cell `(i, j)`, repeatedly moving to a random cell of the current cell's hook until an outside corner is reached; return the coordinates of that final cell. The *hook* of a cell is the cells to its right and below.
algorithm: Random **hook walk** **[GNW84]** (basic tool for random tableau creation).

description: A random standard tableau from `M` of shape `S` (a partition). If `M` is given it must contain more than `Weight(S)` labels.

A (not completely) random standard tableau from `M` of weight `n`. The probability of a given shape `S` is `N_S / n!` (`N_S` = number of standard tableaux of shape `S`), so more populous shapes occur more often. If `M` is given it must contain at least `n` labels.
The (outer) shape of tableau `t`: the partition of decreasing row lengths of its Young diagram.

The skew (inner) shape of `t`: the partition of row lengths of the deleted inner diagram. For a non-skew tableau this is the null sequence. Trailing zeroes are added to match the length of the outer shape.
True if the Young diagram of partition `P₁` covers that of partition `P₂`.
The partition corresponding to the conjugate Young diagram of partition `P` (see §145.4).
The number of non-skew cells in the Young diagram of tableau `t`.
The number of skew cells in the Young diagram of `t`.
The number of rows of `t`.
The number of skewed rows of `t`.
The non-skewed entries of the `i`-th row, as a word of an ordered monoid.
A sequence of words giving the non-skewed entries of all rows.
The non-skewed entries of the `j`-th column, as a word of an ordered monoid.
A sequence of words giving the non-skewed entries of all columns.
The length of the skewed portion of the `i`-th row (zero if none).
The length of the skewed portion of the `j`-th column (zero if none).
The index of the first non-skew entry of the `i`-th row; one greater than the row length if the row has no non-skew entries.
The index of the last entry of the `i`-th row, i.e. the length of the `i`-th row.
The index of the first non-skew entry of the `j`-th column; one greater than the column length if none.
The index of the last entry of the `j`-th column, i.e. the length of the `j`-th column.
For a Young diagram given by tableau `t` or partition `P` and a cell `(i, j)` on it: the *length* of the hook of that cell (number of cells to the right and below, including the cell).
The content of tableau `t`: a sequence of non-negative integers whose `i`-th value is the number of times the `i`-th label occurs in `t`.
The row word of `t`: entries read left to right, bottom to top, as a word of an ordered monoid.
The column word of `t`: labels read bottom to top, left to right, as a word of an ordered monoid.
True iff tableau `t` of weight `n` has exactly the first `n` labels of its parent monoid (equivalently content of the form `[1, 1, …, 1]`).
True if `t` is a skew tableau.
True if `t` is a Littlewood–Richardson tableau, i.e. its content forms a reverse lattice word (see §145.3).
True if tableaux `t1`, `t2` are equal.
The product tableau of `t1` and `t2`, definable by either row insertion or jeu de taquin.
Build a rectangle of empty cells with as many columns as `t1` and as many rows as `t2`; attach `t1` below it and `t2` to its right, giving a skew tableau.
For a tableau `t` with strictly increasing rows: the tableau on the conjugate Young diagram obtained by transposing rows and columns.
For a skew tableau `t` and an *inside corner* `(i, j)` of its skew shape: remove the skewed `(i, j)` cell using *jeu de taquin*.
Remove all skewed cells successively using jeu de taquin (rectification).

For a tableau `t` and coordinates `(i, j)` on its outside resulting in a valid shape: add a new skew cell at `(i, j)` and perform jeu de taquin in reverse, producing a skew tableau of skew degree one higher than `t`.
Insert a word `w` (from the ordered monoid `t` is associated to) or a plactic-monoid element `u` into `t` by Schensted row insertion. For `u`, any word of its Knuth class is used (well defined).

For integer `r > 0` and finite field `K` of cardinality `q`: the `r`-th order Hamming code over `K`, of length `n = (qʳ − 1)/(q − 1)`.
The `[2ʳ − 1, r, 2ʳ⁻¹]` binary simplex code, the dual of a Hamming code.
For `0 ≤ r ≤ m`: the `r`-th order binary Reed–Muller code of length `n = 2ᵐ`.
The block length `n` of the `[n, k]` code `C`.
The dimension `k` of the `[n, k]` linear code `C`.
The number of codewords belonging to `C`.
The information rate `k/n` of the `[n, k]` code `C`.
The ambient space of `C`, i.e. the generic `R`-space `V` containing `C`.
The `[n, k]` code `C` returned as a subspace `U` of `V`, with basis corresponding to the rows of the generator matrix.
The generic `[n, n, 1]` code in which the `[n, k]` code `C` is contained.
The underlying ring (alphabet) `R` of `C`.
The generator matrix for `C`, as an element of `Hom(U, V)`, `U` the information space and `V` the ambient space.
The current vector-space basis of `C`, as a sequence of elements of `C`.
The current vector-space basis of `C`, as a set of elements of `C`.
For `1 ≤ i ≤ k`: the `i`-th element of the current basis of `C`.
The code dual to `C`.
The parity-check matrix for `C`, as an element of `Hom(V, U)`.
The hull of `C`: the intersection of `C` with its dual.

subsection: 152.3.5 The Information Space and Information Sets
description: The `k`-dimensional `R`-space `U` of information vectors for the `[n, k]` code `C`.

subsection: 152.3.5 The Information Space and Information Sets
description: For `C` over a finite field: the current information set — an ordered set of `k` linearly independent columns of the generator matrix on which the matrix restricts to the identity. Returned as a sequence of `k` column indices.

subsection: 152.3.5 The Information Space and Information Sets
description: For `C` over a finite field: all possible information sets, as a sorted sequence of sequences of column indices (each a maximal set of linearly independent columns).

subsection: 152.3.5 The Information Space and Information Sets
description: For `C` over a finite field: the standard form `D` of `C` (the first `k` coordinates correspond to the information set, so the first `k` columns of the generator give the identity), plus an isomorphism from `C` to `D`.
The `(n−k)`-dimensional vector space `W` of syndrome vectors for the `[n, k]` code `C`.
For a cyclic code `C` over a finite field: the generator polynomial of `C`, a divisor of `xⁿ − 1` (`n` the length).
For a cyclic code `C`: the check polynomial `h(x) ∈ K[x]`; with generator `g(x)`, `g(x)h(x) ≡ 0 (mod xⁿ − 1)`.
For a cyclic code `C`: the polynomial idempotent `c(x)` of `C`, satisfying `c(x)² ≡ c(x) (mod xⁿ − 1)`.
For `C ⊆ R⁽ⁿ⁾` and `a₁,…,aₙ ∈ R`: the codeword `(a₁,…,aₙ)` of `C`. It is checked that the vector lies in `C`.
For `u` in the ambient space `V = R⁽ⁿ⁾`: the codeword of `C` corresponding to `u`. Fails if `u ∉ C`.
The zero word of `C`.
A random codeword of `C`.
Sum of codewords `u`, `v` in the same linear code `C`.
Additive inverse of the codeword `u` in `C`.
Difference of codewords `u`, `v` in the same code `C`.
For `a` in the field `K` and codeword `u ∈ C`: the codeword `a * u`.
For non-zero `u ∈ C` over a field: `(1/a) * u`, `a` the first non-zero component of `u`; the result has its first non-zero component equal to the unit of `K`. The zero vector is returned unchanged.
For an `[n, k]` code `C` over a finite field with parent space `V`, and `w ∈ V`: the syndrome of `w` relative to `C` (an element of the syndrome space of `C`).
The Hamming distance between codewords `u`, `v` in the same code `C`.
The Hamming weight of `u` (number of non-zero components).
The Lee weight of the codeword `u`.
Inner product of `u`, `v` (Euclidean norm), where `u`, `v` belong to the parent vector space of `C`.
For a word `w` of the `[n, k]` code `C`: its support as a subset of `{1..n}` (the coordinates where `w` is non-zero).
For codeword `u` of the `[n, k]` code `C`: the coordinates `Q = [a₁,…,aₖ]` over the alphabet of `C` with `u = a₁*C.1 + … + aₖ*C.k`.
For a word `w` of `C`: the ambient space `V` of `C`.
The vector obtained from `u` by cyclically shifting its components to the right by `k` positions.
Destructively rotate `u` by `k` positions.
For `u` with components in `K` and a subfield `S` of `K`: the vector over `S` obtained by taking the trace of each component with respect to `S`. If `S` is omitted, it is the prime field of `K`.
`true` iff the codewords `u`, `v` are equal.
`true` iff the codewords `u`, `v` are not equal.
`true` iff the codeword `u` is the zero vector.
For codeword `u` of `C` over the ring `R`: the `i`-th component of `u` (an element of `R`).
For `u` in a subcode `C` of the full `R`-space `V = Rⁿ`, `1 ≤ i ≤ n`, `x ∈ R`: a vector in `V` equal to `u` with its `i`-th component redefined to be `x`.

For a code `C` with ambient space `V` over a finite field: a set of coset leaders (vectors of minimal weight in their cosets) for `C` in `V`, as an indexed set of vectors from `V`. Only applicable when `V` and `C` are small. Also returns a map from the syndrome space of `C` to the coset leaders.
algorithm: Enumeration of minimal-weight coset representatives; syndrome → leader map.

description: For an `[n, k]` linear code `C` over `R`: the subcode of `C` generated by the items of the list `L`, each one of: (a) an element of `C`; (b) a set/sequence of elements of `C`; (c) a sequence of `n` elements of `R` defining an element of `C`; (d) a set/sequence of such sequences; (e) a subcode of `C`.
For `1 ≤ t < n`: a subcode of `C` of dimension `t`. (Argument named `k`; documented dimension `t`.)
For a set `S` of integers each in `[1, k]`: the subcode generated by the basis elements at the positions in `S`.
For `C1` and a subcode `C2` of `C1`: a subcode of `C1` of dimension `k` containing `C2`.
For an `[n, k]` code `C` and a set `S` of integers in `[1, n]`: the subcode generated by those words of `C` whose weights lie in `S`.
The (vector-space) sum of the linear codes `C` and `D` contained in the same `K`-space `V`.
The intersection of the linear codes `C` and `D` in the same `K`-space `V`.
The dual `D` of `C`: all codewords in `V` orthogonal to every codeword of `C`.
`true` iff the vector `u` of `V` belongs to the code `C`.
`true` iff `u` does not belong to `C`.
`true` iff `C` is a subcode of `D`.
`true` iff `C` is not a subcode of `D`.
`true` iff `C` and `D` are equal.
`true` iff `C` and `D` are not equal.
`true` iff `C` is a cyclic code.
`true` iff `C` is self-dual (`C` equals its dual).
`true` iff `C` is self-orthogonal (`C` is contained in its dual).
`true` iff `C` is maximum-distance separable, i.e. has parameters `[n, k, n−k+1]`.
`true` iff `C` is equidistant.
`true` iff `C` is perfect, i.e. `#C` equals the size of the sphere-packing bound of `C`.
`true` iff the binary linear code `C` is nearly perfect.
`true` iff `C` is an even binary linear code (all codewords have even weight). If `true`, Magma adjusts the minimum-weight bounds of `C` if possible.
`true` iff `C` is a doubly-even binary linear code (all weights divisible by 4). If `true`, Magma adjusts the minimum-weight bounds if possible.
`true` iff the (non-quantum) code `C` is projective.

The minimum weight (= minimum distance) of `C`. Parameters: `Method` (`"Auto"` default, or `"Distribution"` / `"Zimmerman"`), `RankLowerBound` (default 0; minimum rank of information sets used), `MaximumTime` (default ∞; user-time limit after which the calculation is aborted), `Nthreads` (default 1; over `F₂`, number of POSIX threads, alternatively `SetNthreads`).
algorithm: Brouwer–Zimmermann embedding **[BFK+98]**; brute-force `"Distribution"` for small codes. Verbose flag `"Code"` reports progress.

description: The currently known lower and upper bounds on the minimum weight of `C`.
Undefine the known minimum weight of `C` and reset any known bounds.

Run the minimum-weight algorithm until it determines whether `d` is a lower bound on the minimum weight of `C`. Returns: a boolean (`true` iff `d` verified as a lower bound, `false` if aborted on time); the best available lower bound; a boolean (`true` iff that value is the actual minimum weight). Parameters `RankLowerBound` (default 0), `MaximumTime` (default ∞).

As above, but verifying whether `d` is an upper bound on the minimum weight. Returns a boolean, the best available upper bound, and a boolean (`true` iff actual minimum weight). Parameters `RankLowerBound` (default 0), `MaximumTime` (default ∞).
One word of `C` having minimum weight.

The set of all words of `C` having minimum weight. Parameters: `NumWords` (terminate after that many words found), `Method` (`"Auto"` default, or `"Distribution"` / `"Zimmerman"`), `RankLowerBound` (default ∞), `MaximumTime` (default ∞).
algorithm: A variation of the Zimmermann minimum-weight algorithm; brute-force enumeration for small codes. Verbose flag `"Code"`.

description: Include an automorphism `p` (or group `G`) of `C` — a column permutation or a full monomial permutation — in the known-automorphisms subgroup. Automorphisms with long cycles can aid the minimum-weight calculation.
The maximally known subgroup of the full automorphism group of `C`.
The weight distribution of `C`, as a sequence of tuples `(wᵢ, number of codewords of weight wᵢ)`.
The weight distribution of the coset `C + u`, in the same form.
The weight distribution of the dual code of `C`.
The weight distribution of `C` up to the specified upper bound `ub`. Uses the minimum-weight collection to gather word sets.
The Hamming weight enumerator `W_C(x, y) = Σ_{u∈C} x^{n−wt(u)} y^{wt(u)}`.
The Hamming weight enumerator `W_{C+u}(x, y)` of the coset `C + u`.

The complete weight enumerator `W_C(z₀,…,z_{q−1})` where `q = #K`. With `K`'s elements `ω₀,…,ω_{q−1}` (prime field: `ωᵢ = i`; non-prime: `ω₀ = 0`, `ωᵢ = α^{i−1}` for a primitive `α`), and `sᵢ(u)` the number of components of `u` equal to `ωᵢ`: `W_C = Σ_{u∈C} z₀^{s₀(u)} … z_{q−1}^{s_{q−1}(u)}`.
The complete weight enumerator `W_{C+u}(z₀,…,z_{q−1})` of the coset `C + u`.

For a hypothetical `[n, k]` code over a field of cardinality `q` with weight distribution `W` (as from `WeightDistribution`): the weight distribution `W'` of the dual code. `C` need not exist — works on the integer pairs of `W` alone; if `W` is not a genuine weight distribution, `W'` is meaningless (possibly negative weights).

For a hypothetical `[n, k]` code over finite field `K` with complete weight enumerator `W` (as from `CompleteWeightEnumerator`): the complete weight enumerator `W'` of the dual code. Combinatorial transform based on `K`, `n`, `k`, `W` alone.

The set of all words of `C` having weight `w`. Parameters: `NumWords` (terminate after that many words), `Method` (`"Auto"` default, or `"Distribution"` / `"Zimmerman"`), `RankLowerBound` (default ∞), `MaximumTime` (default ∞).
algorithm: Zimmermann minimum-weight-based collection or brute force. Verbose flag `"Code"`.

description: The number of words of `C` having weight `w`.

The set of all words of `C` of weight between `l` and `u` inclusive. Parameters: `Cutoff` (default ∞; terminate after `c` words found), `StoreWords` (default `true`; if true, any words of a single weight generated are stored internally).
The set of all words of `C` of weight `i` consisting of zeros and ones alone.
The number of such constant (zero-one) words of weight `i`.

The coset distance distribution of `C` relative to `C`. The distance between `C` and a coset `D` is the Hamming weight of a minimum-weight vector in `D`. Returned as a sequence of pairs `(d, number of cosets at distance d from C)`.
The covering radius of the linear code `C`.
The diameter of `C` (the largest weight of the codewords of `C`).
For a vector `u ∈ R⁽ⁿ⁾`: the `[n, k]` cyclic code generated by the right cyclic shifts of `u`.

For integer `n > 0`, a set/sequence `T` of primitive `n`-th roots of unity from a finite field `L`, and a subfield `K` of `L`: the cyclic code `C` over `K` of length `n` whose generator polynomial is the least-degree polynomial having the elements of `T` as roots.
algorithm: Minimal polynomial of the root set.

description: The quasicyclic code of length `n` with generator polynomials in the sequence `Gen`. Created by `HorizontalJoin` of each `GeneratorMatrix` from the `CyclicCode`s generated by the polynomials in `Gen`. Requires `|Gen| | n`.
algorithm: Horizontal join of cyclic generator matrices.

description: The quasicyclic code of length `n` generated by simultaneous cyclic shifts of the vectors in `Gen`.
As `QuasiCyclicCode(n, Gen)` but the generator matrices are joined 2-dimensionally with height `h`. Requires `h | (|Gen|)` and `(|Gen|/h) | n`.
The quasicyclic code generated by simultaneous cyclic shifts of the vectors in `Gen`, arranged 2-dimensionally with height `h`.
The length-`n` code generated by consta-cyclic shifts by `α` of the coefficients of `f`.
The quasi-twisted cyclic code of length `n` pasting together the constacyclic codes with parameter `α` generated by the polynomials in `Gen`.
The quasi-twisted cyclic code generated by simultaneous constacyclic shifts w.r.t. `α` of the codewords in `Gen`.

For `K = F_q`, positive integers `n`, `d`, `b` with `gcd(n, q) = 1`: let `m` be least with `n | (qᵐ − 1)` and `α` a primitive `n`-th root of unity in `GF(qᵐ)`. The BCH code of designated distance `d`, the cyclic code with generator `g(x) = lcm{m₁(x), …, m_{d−1}(x)}`, `mᵢ(x)` the minimum polynomial of `α^{b+i−1}`. This is an `[n, ≥ (n − m(d−1)), ≥ d]` code over `K`. If `b` is omitted it is taken to be 1 (a narrow-sense BCH code).
algorithm: Generator = lcm of minimum polynomials of consecutive powers of `α`.

description: For `K = GF(q)`, `G(z)` over `GF(qᵐ)`, and `L = [α₁,…,αₙ]` from `GF(qᵐ)` with `G(αᵢ) ≠ 0`: the Goppa code `Γ(L, G)` over `K`. If `deg G = r`, this is an `[n, k ≥ n − mr, d ≥ r + 1]` code.

For polynomials `P`, `G` over a finite field `F`, integer `n > 1`, subfield `S` of `F` with `n` coprime to `#S`, `F` the splitting field of `xⁿ − 1` over `S`, `P` and `G` coprime to `xⁿ − 1` and of degree `< n`: the Chien–Choy generalised BCH code with parameters `P`, `G`, `n` over `S`.

For `A = [α₁,…,αₙ]` distinct, from the degree-`m` extension `K` of finite field `S`, `Y = [y₁,…,yₙ]` non-zero from `K`, positive integer `r`: the alternant code `A(A, Y)` over `S`, an `[n, k ≥ n − mr, d ≥ r + 1]` code. If `S` is omitted, it is the prime subfield of `K`.
The `[n, k, d]` non-primitive alternant code over `F₂`, with `n − mr ≤ k ≤ n − r` and `d ≥ r + 1`.
For `K = GF(q)`, `h ∈ K[X]`, non-negative integer `s`, positive integer `n`: a Fire code of length `n` with generator polynomial `h(Xˢ − 1)`.
For `A = [a₁,…aₙ]`, `W = [w₁,…wₛ]` with the `n+s` elements of `A`, `W` distinct and `Z = [z₁,…zₖ]` non-zero, and positive integer `t`: the Gabidulin MDS code with parameters `A, W, Z, t`.

For `A = [α₁,…,αₙ]`, `W = [w₁,…,wₛ]` from the extension `K` of `S`, with `A` non-zero and the `n+s` elements of `A`, `W` distinct, and integer `μ`: the Srivastava code of parameters `A, W, μ` over `S`.

For `A = [α₁,…,αₙ]`, `W = [w₁,…,wₛ]`, `Z = [z₁,…zₖ]` from the extension `K` of `S`, with `A`, `Z` non-zero, the `n+s` elements of `A`, `W` distinct, positive integer `t`: the generalized Srivastava code with parameters `A, W, Z, t` over `S`.

subsection: 152.9.3 Quadratic Residue Codes and their Generalizations
description: For `K = F_q` and an odd prime `n` such that `q` is a quadratic residue mod `n`: the quadratic residue code of length `n` over `K`. The cyclic code with generator `g₀(x) = ∏ (x − αʳ)`, `α` a primitive `n`-th root of unity in some extension, the product over all quadratic residues mod `p`.
algorithm: Cyclic code with QR root set.

subsection: 152.9.3 Quadratic Residue Codes and their Generalizations
description: For `K = GF(2)`: the binary Golay code; for `K = GF(3)`: the ternary Golay code. If `ext` is `true`, the extended code in each case.

subsection: 152.9.3 Quadratic Residue Codes and their Generalizations
description: For an odd prime `p`: the doubly-circulant binary `[2p, p]` code based on quadratic residues mod `p` (generator matrix `[I | A]`, `A` circulant).

subsection: 152.9.3 Quadratic Residue Codes and their Generalizations
description: For a prime power `m > 2` and `a ∈ {0, 1}`: a `[2m, m]` doubly-circulant linear code over `GF(4)`. See **[Gab02]**.

subsection: 152.9.3 Quadratic Residue Codes and their Generalizations
description: For an odd prime `p` and integers `a`, `b`: the bordered doubly-circulant binary `[2p+1, p+1]` code based on quadratic residues mod `p`; the first `p` rows are extended by `a mod 2` and the `(p+1)`-th row by `b mod 2`.

subsection: 152.9.3 Quadratic Residue Codes and their Generalizations
description: For positive integers `l`, `m` both coprime to 2: a binary "twisted QR" code of length `l*m`.

subsection: 152.9.3 Quadratic Residue Codes and their Generalizations
description: For `K = F_q`, positive integer `n` and prime `p` such that `q` is a `p`-th power residue mod `n`: the `p`-th power residue code of length `n`.

For `K = F_q` and positive integer `d`: the Reed–Solomon code of length `n = q − 1` and design distance `d`. Equals `BCHCode(K, q−1, d)`. See **[MS78, p.294]**. If `b` is given (non-negative integer), the primitive element is first raised to the `b`-th power.
algorithm: BCH code over `F_q` of full length. **[MS78]**.

description: For integer `n` with `q = n + 1` a prime power and positive integer `d`: the Reed–Solomon code over `F_q` of length `n` and designed minimum distance `d`. If `b` is given, the primitive element is first raised to the `b`-th power.

For `A = [α₁,…,αₙ]` distinct from finite field `K`, `V = [v₁,…,vₙ]` non-zero from `K`, and non-negative integer `k`: the generalized Reed–Solomon code `GRS_k(A, V)` over `K`, an `[n, k' ≤ k]` code. See **[MS78, p.303]**.
For `N = 2ᵐ − 1` and positive integer `K`: the binary linear Justesen code of length `2mN` and dimension `mK`. See **[MS78, p.307]**.
For `GF(q = 2ᵐ)`: the `[q + 1, k, q − k + 2]` maximum distance separable code.
For an `[n, k]` binary code `C`: a new code `C'` including the all-ones vector with the words of `C` (if not already in `C`).
For a subcode `C1` of `C`: a code `C2` with `C = C1 + C2`.
For `[n₁, k₁]` code `C` and `[n₂, k₂]` code `D` over the same field: the direct sum, all vectors `u|v` with `u ∈ C`, `v ∈ D`.
For a sequence `Q = [C₁,…,C_r]` of codes over the same field: their direct sum.
For `[n₁, k₁]` code `C` and `[n₂, k₂]` code `D` over the same ring `R`: the direct product, of length `n₁·n₂`, dimension `k₁·k₂`, with generator the Kronecker product of the basis matrices.
For an `[n, k, d]` code `C`: a new code `C'` adding the coordinate making each codeword's coordinate sum zero (binary: appends a 0 to even-weight words and a 1 to odd-weight words).
The code `C` extended `n` times.
Add `n` zeros to the end of each codeword of `C`.
A new code by deleting all codewords of `C` having odd weight.
For a sequence `L` of codewords from `C`: the result of deleting the words in `L` from `C`.
Delete a subspace generated by a word of weight `w`.
For an `[n, k]` binary code `C`: a new code by first adding the all-ones codeword, then extending by an overall parity check.
For two codes over the same alphabet: all vectors `u|u + v` with `u ∈ C1`, `v ∈ C2` (zeros appended to make up length differences). An `[n₁ + max{n₁,n₂}, k₁ + k₂, min{2d₁, d₂}]` code.

For three codes over the same alphabet: all vectors `u|u + a*v|u + v + w`, `u ∈ C1`, `v ∈ C2`, `w ∈ C3` (zeros appended for length differences). Parameter `a` (FldFinElt, default `−1`). For `a = −1`, an `[n₁ + max{n₁,n₂} + max{n₁,n₂,n₃}, k₁ + k₂ + k₃, min{3d₁, 2d₂, d₃}]` code.
For an `[n, k]` code `C` and `1 ≤ i ≤ n`: a new code `C'` deleting the `i`-th coordinate from each codeword.
For a set `S` of distinct integers in `[1, n]`: delete the components `i₁,…,iᵣ` from each codeword.
For an `[n, k]` code `C` and `1 ≤ i ≤ n`: select the codewords with a zero `i`-th component and delete that component; resulting length `n − 1`.
For a set `S` of distinct integers in `[1, n]`: select codewords with zeros in all positions `i₁,…,iᵣ` and delete those components; resulting length `n − r`.

subsection: 152.10.2 Changing the Alphabet of a Code
description: For an `[n, k, d]` code `C` over `K` and extension field `L` of `K`: the code `C'` over `L` corresponding to `C`, plus the embedding map.

subsection: 152.10.2 Changing the Alphabet of a Code
description: For an `[n, k, d]` code `C` over `K` and a subfield `S` of `K` with `[K : S] = m`: a new `[N = mn, k, D ≥ d]` code `C'` over `S` replacing each component of each codeword by its representation as a vector over `S`. Also returns the isomorphism from `C` onto `C'`.

subsection: 152.10.2 Changing the Alphabet of a Code
description: For a code over `GF(qᵐ)`: a code whose codewords are obtained by expanding each coordinate in `GF(qᵐ)` as a dimension-`m` vector over `K = GF(q)`.

subsection: 152.10.2 Changing the Alphabet of a Code
description: As above but expanding each coordinate as a dimension-`m+1` vector over `K = GF(q)`, including a parity-check bit.

subsection: 152.10.2 Changing the Alphabet of a Code
description: For an `[n, k, d]` code `C` over `K` and subfield `S`: a new `[n, K ≤ k, D ≥ d]` code `C'` over `S` of the codewords of `C` having all components in `S`. If `S` is omitted, the prime subfield of `K`. Also returns the restriction map.

subsection: 152.10.2 Changing the Alphabet of a Code
description: For an `[n, k]` code `C` over `K` and subfield `S` with `[K : S] = m`: a new `[n, k']` code over `S` expanding each element of `K` as a column vector over `S`; `k' ≤ km`.

subsection: 152.10.2 Changing the Alphabet of a Code
description: For a code `C` over `K` and subfield `F`: a new code `C'` over `F` of the traces with respect to `F` of each codeword. If `F` is omitted, the prime subfield of `K`.
For codes `C1`, `C2` over the same field `K` with generator matrices `A`, `B`: the concatenation, the code whose generator rows are each row of `A` concatenated with each row of `B`.
For `[n₁, k, d₁]` code `C1` and `[n₂, k, d₂]` code `C2` of the same dimension over the same field `K`: an `[n₁ + n₂, k, ≥ d₁ + d₂]` code with generator `HorizontalJoin(A, B)`.
For an `[N, K, D]` code `O` over `GF(qᵏ)` (outer) and an `[n, k, d]` code `I` over `GF(q)` (inner): the `[Nn, Kk, δ ≥ dD]` concatenated code.

For `C1 = [n₁, k₁, d₁]`, `C2 = [n₂, k₂, d₂]` (`C2` a union of `b` cosets of `C1`, so `n₁ = n₂` and `k₂ ≤ k₁`), `C3 = [n₃, k₃, d₃]` with `k₁ = k₂ + k₃`: divide `C2` into cosets of `C1` and attach a different codeword of `C3` to each coset. The new code has parameters `[n₁ + n₃, k₁, ≥ min{d₂, d₁ + d₃}]`. See **[MS78, p.581]**.
For a sequence `S` of codes all subcodes of the first, apply `ConstructionX` to `S[1]`, `S[2]`, `C`, then compute the resulting subcodes from the other codes in `S`.

For a chain `C1 = [n, k₁, d₁]`, `C2 = [n, k₂, d₂]`, `C3 = [n, k₃, d₃]` with `k₃ < k₂ < k₁`, and suffix codes `D1 = [n₁, k₁ − k₂, e₁]`, `D2 = [n₂, k₃ − k₂, e₂]`: a code `[n + n₁ + n₂, k₁, ≥ min{d₃, d₁ + e₁, d₂ + e₂}]`. See **[MS78, p.583]**.

For two chains `C1 = [n, k₁] ⊂ C2 = [n, k₂] ⊂ C3 = [n, k₃]` and `D1 = [n', k₁ − k₃] ⊂ D2 = [n', k₂ − k₃]`: returns `C = [n + n', k₁] ⊂ C' = [n + n', k₂]` using Construction X with `C1, C3, D1` resp. `C2, C3, D2`.

For codes `C1 = [n₁, k, d₁]`, `C2 = [n₁, k − l₂, d₂]`, `C3 = [n₁, k − l₃, d₃]` (`C2`, `C3` subcodes of `C1`), and `D2 = [n₂, l₂, δ₂]`, `D3 = [n₃, l₃, δ₃]`: break `C1` into cosets of `C2`, `C3` with tails from `D2`, `D3`. If `C1 ∩ C2` has minimum distance `d₀`, parameters `[n₁ + n₂ + n₃, k, min{d₀, d₂ + δ₂, d₃ + δ₃, d₁ + δ₂ + δ₃}]`. See **[All84]**.

A generalised concatenated code. `I` is an increasing chain of `r` inner codes `[n, k₁, d₁]_q ⊂ … ⊂ [n, k_r, d_r]_q` (`0 = k₀ < k₁ < … < k_r`); `O` is a sequence of `r` outer codes `[N, Kᵢ, Dᵢ]_{Qᵢ}` with `Qᵢ = q^{eᵢ}`, `eᵢ = kᵢ − k_{i−1}`. Constructs an `[n*N, K, D]_q` code with `K = e₁K₁ + … + e_rK_r`, `D = min{d₁D₁,…,d_rD_r}`. See **[MS78, p.590]**.

Apply Construction Y1 to `C`: shorten at the positions in the support of a minimal-weight word in the dual of `C`. If `C` is `[n, k, d]` with dual minimum weight `d'`, the result is `[n − d', k − d' + 1, ≥ d]`. See **[MS78, p.592]**.
Apply Construction Y1 to `C`, shortening at the positions in the support of a word of weight `w` in the dual of `C`. If `C` is `[n, k, d]`, the result is `[n − w, k − w + 1, ≥ d]`.

The original McEliece decoding attack: random information sets are tested for being disjoint from the support of the desired error vector. Attempts to enumerate a vector of weight `e` from the error coset `v + C`. Parameters: `MaxTime` (default ∞; aborts if too long), `DirectEnumeration` (default `true`; whether to enumerate the coset directly or the larger code generated by ⟨C, v⟩).

The Lee–Brickell attack: random information sets are tested for having weight ≤ `p` (optimal `p = 2` for most codes). Attempts to enumerate a vector of weight `e` from `v + C`. Parameters `MaxTime`, `DirectEnumeration` (default `true`).

Leon's attack: for random information sets of size `k`, a punctured code of length `k + l` is searched for codewords of weight ≤ `p`. Optimal (small codes, length ≲ 200): `p = 2`, `l ∈ 3–6`; larger codes `p = 3`, `l ∈ 7–10`. Parameters `MaxTime`, `DirectEnumeration` (default `true`).

Stern's attack: a punctured code of length `k + l` is split into two subspaces, each enumerated up to weight `p`, with collisions found at zero non-information weight. Optimal (length ≲ 500): `p = 2`, `l ∈ 9–13`; larger `p = 3`, `l` from 20 up. Parameters `MaxTime`, `DirectEnumeration` (default `true`).

The Canteaut–Chabaud attack: like Stern's but a different linear-algebra process steps through information sets more quickly, at the cost of less independent information sets. Optimal (length ≲ 1000): `p = 1`, `l ∈ 6–9`; very large codes `p = 2`, `l` from 20 up. Parameters `MaxTime`, `DirectEnumeration` (default `true`).

A generalized decoding attack with user-specified enumeration and matrix-sequence procedures; enumerates a vector of weight `e` from `v + C`. Parameters: `Enumeration` (`"Standard"` default, `"Leon"`, `"HashTable"` — the methods of Lee–Brickell, Leon, Stern); `MatrixSequence` (`"Random"` default, or `"Stepped"`); `NumSteps` (default 1; generalised stepped process with sets differing in this many places); `p` (default 2); `l` (enumeration parameter); `MaxTime` (default ∞); `DirectEnumeration` (default `true`). For lengths 500–1000, best performance with a multiply-stepped sequence (~10 steps), hashtable enumeration, `p = 2`, `l ∈ 15–20`.
algorithm: Generalised two-stage information-set decoding combining the standard attacks.

For alternant codes the Euclidean algorithm is the default but `Al := "Syndrome"` forces syndrome decoding; for non-alternant codes only syndrome decoding is possible (the Euclidean method cannot correct as many errors as syndrome decoding but is much faster).

For a set/sequence `S` of codes of length `n` and `x` in a permutation group: the set/sequence of images of the codes under `x`.

description: The permutation group `G` of the `[n, k]` code `C` over `K`: all permutation-action permutations preserving the code (degree `n`). Also returns a power structure `P` and transfer map `t`.

section: 153.2 Creation of an Algebraic Geometric Code
description: For `X` an irreducible plane curve, `S` a sequence of degree-1 places of `X`, and `D` a divisor whose support is disjoint from the support of `S`: the (weakly) algebraic–geometric code obtained by evaluating functions of the Riemann–Roch space of `D` at the points of `S`. The degree of `D` need not be bounded by the cardinality of `S`.
algorithm: Evaluation of an `L(D)` basis at the places of `S` (Hess function-field divisor machinery) **[Sti93, TV91]**.

section: 153.2 Creation of an Algebraic Geometric Code
description: The dual of the algebraic geometric code constructed from the sequence of places `S` and the divisor `D`; corresponds to a differential code. To exploit the algebraic geometric structure, the dual must be constructed this way and **not** by directly calling `Dual`.
algorithm: Differential / residue construction of the dual AG code.

section: 153.2 Creation of an Algebraic Geometric Code
description: For prime power `q` and positive integer `r`: a Hermitian code `C` with respect to the Hermitian curve `X = x^(q+1) + y^(q+1) + z^(q+1)` defined over `F_{q²}`. The support consists of all degree-1 places of `X` over `F_{q²}`, except the place over `P = (1 : 1 : 0)`; the divisor used to define the Riemann–Roch space is `r * P`.
algorithm: AG-code construction on the Hermitian curve.

description: Returns `true` iff `C` is a weakly algebraic–geometric code, i.e. `C` was constructed as an algebraic–geometric code with respect to a divisor of any degree.
Returns `true` iff `C` was constructed as the dual of a weakly algebraic–geometric code.
Returns `true` iff `C` is of algebraic–geometric construction of length `n`, built from a divisor `D` with `deg(D) < n`.
Returns `true` iff `C` is an algebraic–geometric code of length `n` constructed from a divisor `D` satisfying `2g − 2 < deg(D) < n`, where `g` is the genus of the curve.
algorithm: Attribute test plus the strong (Riemann–Roch) degree condition.

description: The curve from which `C` was defined.
The sequence of places which forms the support for `C`.
The divisor from which `C` was constructed.
For `C` constructed from a divisor `D`: the Goppa designed distance `n − deg(D)`.
Decode the received vector `v` of the dual algebraic geometric code `C` using the divisor `Fd`.
algorithm: Specialized differential-code (basic algorithm) decoding using an auxiliary divisor.

description: The linear code `C` over `F_q` associated with the lattice points of the polygon `P`. After a translation so that the lattice points of `P` lie in the first quadrant as close to the origin as possible, the points must lie in the box `[0, q−2] × [0, q−2]`. The code is the monomial evaluation code where each point `(a, b)` corresponds to the monomial `x^a y^b`, evaluated at the points of the torus `(F_q*)²`.
The linear code `C` over `F_q` associated with the lattice points in `S` (a set or sequence). As usual, the points are translated to lie within a box at the origin of the first quadrant.
Given a sparse binary matrix `H`, return the LDPC code which has `H` as its parity check matrix.
algorithm: Direct construction from the assigned sparse parity check matrix.

description: Return a random `(a, b)`-regular LDPC code of length `n`. The row weight `a` must divide the length `n`.
Return a random code from the ensemble of `(a, b)`-regular binary LDPC codes.
algorithm: Random selection from the regular ensemble.

description: Given (unnormalized) distributions `Sv` and `Sc` for the variable and check weights, return a length-`n` irregular LDPC code whose degree distributions match the given distribution. `Sv`, `Sc` are sequences of real numbers, where the `i`-th entry indicates the percentage of variable (resp. check) nodes that should have weight `i`. Distributions are not matched perfectly unless everything is in complete balance.
algorithm: Random selection matching the prescribed degree distributions.

description: Return the `(3,6)`-regular binary LDPC code of length `2(p³ − p)` using the group-based construction of Margulis.
Return `true` if `C` is an LDPC code (i.e. if it has been assigned an LDPC matrix).
Given a sparse matrix `H` which is a parity check matrix of the code `C`, assign `H` as the LDPC matrix of `C`.
Given an LDPC code `C`, return the sparse matrix which has been assigned as its low density parity check matrix.
Given an LDPC code `C`, return the density of the sparse matrix which has been assigned as its low density parity check matrix.
Return `true` if `C` is an LDPC code and has regular column and row weights. If `true`, the row and column weights are also returned.
For an LDPC code `C`, return its Tanner graph. If there are `n` variables and `m` checks, the graph has `n + m` nodes, the first `n` of which are the variable nodes.
For an LDPC code `C`, return the girth of its Tanner graph.
Return the theoretical rate of LDPC codes from the ensemble described by the given inputs (either two integers for a `(v, c)`-regular ensemble, or two density distributions `Sv`, `Sc`).
algorithm: Theoretical ensemble rate from the degree distributions.

description: For an LDPC code `C` and a received vector `v`, decode `v` to a codeword of `C` using the LDPC iterative decoding algorithm. The channel is described by `Channel` (`"BinarySymmetric"` (default) or `"Gaussian"`); errors on the binary symmetric channel are described by `p` (default `0.1`), on the Gaussian channel by `StdDev` (default `0.25`). `v` must be over a ring corresponding to the channel: a binary vector over `F₂` for the binary symmetric channel, real-valued for the Gaussian channel. `Iterations` (default `Dimension(C)`) sets the maximum number of iterations; the default is much larger than normally used in practice, giving maximum error-correcting performance at possible cost to efficiency.

For an LDPC code `C`, simulate `N` transmissions across the given channel and return the accumulated bit error rate and word error rate. Variable arguments (`Channel` default `"BinarySymmetric"`, `p` default `0.1`, `StdDev` default `0.25`, `Iterations` default `Dimension(C)`) are as for `LDPCDecode`; the channel controls both the decoding algorithm and the nature of the errors introduced during simulation.
algorithm: Repeated channel simulation plus iterative decoding.

description: Determine the threshold of the described ensemble over the binary symmetric channel — the critical channel-parameter value above which there is a non-vanishing (asymptotic) error probability. The ensemble may be given by two integers for a `(v, c)`-regular code, or by two density distributions `Sv`, `Sc` (sequences of non-negative reals, not necessarily normalized; the first entry, corresponding to weight-1 nodes in the Tanner graph, should always be zero). `Precision` (default `0.00005`) controls the precision of the threshold.
algorithm: Establishes lower and upper bounds on the threshold, then narrows the range by repeatedly performing density evolution on the midpoint.

description: Perform density evolution on the binary symmetric channel using channel parameter `p` and determine the asymptotic behaviour for the given LDPC ensemble. Returns a boolean; `true` indicates `p` is below the threshold and the ensemble has error probability asymptotically tending to zero.
algorithm: Density evolution at the single channel parameter `p`.

description: Determine the threshold of the described ensemble over the Gaussian channel — the critical standard-deviation value above which there is a non-vanishing (asymptotic) error probability. Ensemble given by two integers `(v, c)` or by two density distributions `Sv`, `Sc` (non-negative reals, first entry zero). `Lower` (default `0`) / `Upper` (default `∞`): real-valued bounds on the threshold that, if tight, reduce the search range (validity verified before the search; error if incorrect). `Points` (default `500`) / `MaxLLR` (default `25`): define the discretized basis of log likelihood ratios on which density evolution is performed — the probability mass function is defined on `[−MaxLLR, …, MaxLLR]` over `2·Points + 1` discretized points. `MaxIterations` (default `∞`): finite limit on iterations per channel parameter (may speed computation but result may not be valid). `QuickCheck` (default `true`): selects how asymptotic behaviour is identified — if `false`, the density must evolve to within an infinitesimal of unity; if `true`, behaviour is assumed to go to unity once the rate of change is successively increasing (empirically accurate but without theoretical justification). `Precision` (default `0.00005`): precision of the threshold. Verbose mode `Code` prints the threshold bounds as evolutions narrow the range.
algorithm: Establishes lower and upper bounds on the threshold, then narrows by repeated density evolution on the midpoint over the discretized LLR basis.

description: Perform density evolution on the Gaussian channel using standard deviation `σ` and determine the asymptotic behaviour for the given LDPC ensemble. Returns a boolean; `true` indicates `σ` is below the threshold and the ensemble has error probability asymptotically tending to zero. Variable arguments (`Points` default `500`, `MaxLLR` default `25`, `MaxIterations` default `∞`, `QuickCheck` default `true`) are as for `LDPCGaussianThreshold`.
algorithm: Density evolution at the single standard deviation `σ`.

description: Access a small database of density distributions defining good irregular LDPC ensembles. Returns the published threshold of the ensemble over the Gaussian channel, along with the variable and check degree distributions. The input `i` is a non-negative integer indexing the database (in no particular order).
algorithm: Lookup in a built-in database of published good ensembles.

description: Create a code as a subspace of the `R`-space `V = R⁽ⁿ⁾` generated by the items in list `L`. The Delsarte–Goethals code of length `2ᵐ`.
The Goethals–Delsarte code of length `2ᵐ`.
For a prime `p` with 2 a quadratic residue mod `p`: the quadratic residue code of length `p` over **Z₄**.
The Golay code over **Z₄**; if `e` is `true`, the extended Golay code.
The simplex alpha code over **Z₄** of degree `k`.
The simplex beta code over **Z₄** of degree `k`.

For `m ≥ 2` and `1 ≤ δ ≤ ⌊(m+1)/2⌋`: a Hadamard code over **Z₄** of length `2ᵐ⁻¹` and type `2^γ 4^δ` where `γ = m + 1 − 2δ`; also returns a generator matrix with `γ + δ` rows. After the Gray map gives a binary code with the same parameters as the binary Hadamard code of length `2ᵐ`.

For `m ≥ 2` and `1 ≤ δ ≤ ⌊(m+1)/2⌋`: an extended perfect code over **Z₄** of length `2ᵐ⁻¹` whose dual is of type `2^γ 4^δ` with `γ = m + 1 − 2δ`; also returns a generator matrix. After the Gray map gives a binary code with the same parameters as the binary extended perfect code of length `2ᵐ`.

For `m ≥ 2` and `0 ≤ r ≤ m`: the `r`-th order Reed–Muller code over **Z₄** of length `2ᵐ`. Binary image under mod-2 map is the binary linear `r`-th order Reed–Muller code; for `r = 1` / `r = m − 2` returns the quaternary Kerdock / Preparata code respectively.

For `m ≥ 1` and `0 ≤ r ≤ m`: a *set* of `r`-th order Reed–Muller codes over **Z₄** of length `2ᵐ⁻¹`. Gray image of any has the same parameters as the binary linear `r`-th order RM code of length `2ᵐ` (neither the usual inclusion nor duality properties need hold).

For `m ≥ 1`, `0 ≤ r ≤ m`, and `0 ≤ s ≤ ⌊(m−1)/2⌋`: an `r`-th order Reed–Muller code over **Z₄** of length `2ᵐ⁻¹`, denoted `RM_s(r, m)`. Gray image has same parameters as binary RM. Satisfies `RM_s(r−1, m) ⊆ RM_s(r, m)` (`r > 0`), and `RM_s(r, m)` is the Kronecker dual of `RM_s(m − r − 1, m)` (`r < m`).

For `m ≥ 1` and `0 ≤ s ≤ ⌊(m−1)/2⌋`: the family of Reed–Muller codes over **Z₄** of length `2ᵐ⁻¹` — the codes `RM_s(r, m)` for `0 ≤ r ≤ m`. Gray images give a family with same parameters as the binary RM family of length `2ᵐ`; `RM_s(0, m) ⊂ RM_s(1, m) ⊂ … ⊂ RM_s(m, m)`.
For a quaternary code `C`: the binary code formed by reducing each codeword of `C` modulo 2 (the *binary residue code*).
For a quaternary code `C`: the binary code formed by the supports of the codewords of `C` that are zero modulo 2 (the *binary torsion code*).
For binary codes `C₁ ⊂ C₂`: a quaternary code whose binary residue code is `C₁` and binary torsion code is `C₂`.
algorithm: Construct a quaternary lift of the chain (non-unique).

description: For any **Z₄**-linear code `C`: a permutation-equivalent code `S` in standard form, together with the isomorphism from `C` onto `S`.
For matrices `A`, `B` over the same ring with the same number of columns: the matrix `P_AB = [[A, A], [0, B]]`.

For codes `C`, `D` over the same ring and of the same length: the Plotkin sum — all vectors `(u | u + v)`, `u ∈ C`, `v ∈ D`. Returns the code generated by `P_AB` where `A`, `B` are generator matrices of `C`, `D`.
For matrices `A`, `B` over **Z₄** with the same number of columns: `QP_AB = [[A, A, A, A], [0, B, 2B, 3B]]`.
For codes `C`, `D` over **Z₄** of the same length: the Quaternary Plotkin sum — all vectors `(u, u + v, u + 2v, u + 3v)`, `u ∈ C`, `v ∈ D`.

For matrices `A`, `B`, `C` over **Z₄** with the same number of columns: `BQP_ABC = [[A,A,A,A],[0,B',2B',3B'],[0,0,B̂,B̂],[0,0,0,C]]`, where `B'` is `B` with the twos replaced by ones in the rows of order two, and `B̂` is `B` with the rows of order two removed.

For codes `D`, `E`, `F` over **Z₄** of the same length: the BQ Plotkin sum — all vectors `(u, u + v', u + 2v' + v̂, u + 3v' + v̂ + z)`, with `u ∈ Gd`, `v' ∈ Ge'`, `v̂ ∈ Ĝe`, `z ∈ Gf`. **Note:** does not necessarily equal the code generated by the matrix `BQPlotkinSum` of the generator matrices (see H155E14).
For matrices `A`, `B`, `C`, `D` over **Z₄** with the same number of columns: `DP_ABCD = [[A,A,A,A],[0,B,2B,3B],[0,0,C,C],[0,0,0,D]]`.

For codes `E`, `F`, `G`, `H` over **Z₄** of the same length: all vectors `(u, u + v, u + 2v + z, u + 3v + z + t)`, `u ∈ E`, `v ∈ F`, `z ∈ G`, `t ∈ H`. Returns the code generated by `DP_ABCD` of the generator matrices.

For a code `C` over **Z₄** of length `2ᵐ`: its Kronecker dual code `C⊥_⊗ = { x ∈ Z₄^{2ᵐ} : x·K_{2ᵐ}·yᵗ = 0 ∀ y ∈ C }`, where `K_{2ᵐ} = ⊗ⱼ K₂`, `K₂ = [[1,0],[0,3]]`, `⊗` the Kronecker product. Equivalently `K_{2ᵐ}` is a quaternary matrix with `(1,3,3,1,3,1,1,3,…)` on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere.

For a code `C` over **Z₄** of length `n`: `S_C = Φ⁻¹(S_bin)` as a code over **Z₄**, and the linear span `S_bin = ⟨C_bin⟩` as a binary linear code of length `2n`, where `C_bin = Φ(C)` and `Φ` is the Gray map.
algorithm: Linear span of the Gray image, pulled back.

description: For a code `C` over **Z₄** of length `n`: its kernel `K_C` as a subcode over **Z₄** of `C`, and `K_bin = Φ(K_C)` as a binary linear subcode of `C_bin` of length `2n`. The kernel `K_C` is the codewords `v` with `2v∗u ∈ C` for all `u ∈ C` (`∗` componentwise product); equivalently `K_bin` contains `c ∈ C_bin` with `c + C_bin = C_bin`.
For a code `C` over **Z₄**: the dimension of the linear span of `C_bin`, i.e. `dim ⟨C_bin⟩`.
For a code `C` over **Z₄**: the dimension of the Gray-map image of its kernel `K_C`, i.e. `dim K_bin = dim Φ(K_C)`. `K_bin` is always a binary linear code.
For a codeword `v` over **Z₄**: with `wⱼ = #{k : v[k] = j}` for `j = 0,…,3`, the *correlation* of `v` is the Gaussian integer `(w₀ − w₂) + i∗(w₁ − w₃)`.

description: For a length `n` linear code `C` over `R`: the subcode of `C` generated by the items in list `L`. algorithm: Subcode generated by the supplied elements.

description: For a length `n` linear code `C` with `k` generators and `1 ≤ t < k`: a subcode of `C` of pseudo-dimension `t`.

description: For a length `n` linear code `C` with `k` generators and a set `S` of integers in `[1, k]`: the subcode of `C` generated by the basis elements whose positions appear in `S`.
The minimum (Hamming) weight of the words of `C`, equal to the minimum distance between any two codewords.
The (Hamming) weight distribution of `C`, as a sequence of tuples `⟨wᵢ, number of codewords of weight wᵢ⟩`.
The (Hamming) weight distribution of the dual code of `C`.
The Lee weight of the element `a ∈ Z₄`.
The Lee weight of the codeword `v`.
The Lee distance between codewords `u`, `v` of the same code `C` — the Lee weight of `u − v`.
The minimum Lee weight of `C`.
The Lee weight distribution of `C`.
The Lee weight distribution of the dual of `C`.
The set of all words of `C` of Lee weight `w`. Parameter `Cutoff` (`RngIntElt`, default `∞`): if set to a non-negative integer `c`, terminate after `c` words found.
The set of all words of `C` with Lee weight between `l` and `u` inclusive. Parameter `Cutoff` (`RngIntElt`, default `∞`): terminate after `c` words found.
The Euclidean weight of the element `a ∈ Z₄`.
The Euclidean weight of the **Z₄**-codeword `v`.
The Euclidean distance between **Z₄**-codewords `u`, `v` of the same code — the Euclidean weight of `u − v`.
The minimum Euclidean weight of the **Z₄**-code `C`.
The Euclidean weight distribution of the **Z₄**-code `C`.
The Euclidean weight distribution of the dual of the **Z₄**-code `C`.

For `C` over a finite ring `R` of cardinality `q` (elements ordered): the complete weight enumerator `W_C(X₀,…,X_{q−1}) = Σ_{v∈C} X₀^{s₀(v)} X₁^{s₁(v)} ⋯ X_{q−1}^{s_{q−1}(v)}`, where `sᵢ(v)` is the number of components of `v` equal to the `i`-th ring element. Lies in a global multivariate polynomial ring over **Z** with `q` variables (angle-bracket naming allowed). See **[Wan97, p. 9]**.
For a **Z₄**-code `C`: the symmetric weight enumerator `swe_C(X₀,X₁,X₂) = W_C(X₀,X₁,X₂,X₁)`. Lies in a global polynomial ring over **Z** with three variables. See **[Wan97, p. 14]**.
For `C` over a finite ring `R`: the Hamming weight enumerator `Ham_C(X,Y) = Σ_{v∈C} X^{n−w_H(v)} Y^{w_H(v)}`. Two variables, global polynomial ring over **Z**.
For a **Z₄**-code `C`: the Lee weight enumerator `Lee_C(X,Y) = Σ_{v∈C} X^{2n−w_L(v)} Y^{w_L(v)}` (`w_L` from §155.6.2). Two variables.
For a **Z₄**-code `C`: the Euclidean weight enumerator `Euclidean_C(X,Y) = Σ_{v∈C} X^{4n−w_E(v)} Y^{w_E(v)}` (`w_E` from §155.6.3). Two variables.
The (vector-space) sum of the linear codes `C` and `D` (both in the same `R`-space `V`).
The intersection of the linear codes `C` and `D` (both in the same `R`-space `V`).
The dual `D` of the linear code `C`: all codewords in `V` orthogonal to all codewords of `C`.
For a length `n₁` code `C` and length `n₂` code `D` over the same ring `R`: the direct sum — all length `n₁ + n₂` vectors `u|v`, `u ∈ C`, `v ∈ D`.
For a length `n₁` code `C` and length `n₂` code `D` over the same ring `R`: the direct product of length `n₁·n₂` whose generator matrix is the Kronecker product of the basis matrices of `C` and `D`.
For codes `C1`, `C2` over the same ring `R`: the concatenation — generator matrix whose rows are each row of `A` concatenated with each row of `B` (`A`, `B` the generator matrices).
For a length `n` code `C`: a new code `C'` by adding one coordinate to each vector so that the sum of the extended vector's coordinates is zero.
The code `C` extended `n` times.
Add `n` zeros to the end of each codeword of `C`.
For codes `C`, `D` over the same ring `R` and of the same length `n`: the Plotkin sum — all vectors `u | u + v`, `u ∈ C`, `v ∈ D`.
For a length `n` code `C` and `1 ≤ i ≤ n`: a new code `C'` by deleting the `i`-th coordinate from each codeword.
For a length `n` code `C` and a set `S = {i₁,…,i_r}` of distinct integers in `[1, n]`: a new code by deleting the components `i₁,…,i_r` from each codeword.
For a length `n` code `C` and `1 ≤ i ≤ n`: a new code from those codewords of `C` with a zero in their `i`-th component, with the `i`-th component deleted; the result has length `n − 1`.

For a length `n` code `C` and a set `S = {i₁,…,i_r}` of distinct integers in `[1, n]`: a new code from those codewords with zeros in all positions `i₁,…,i_r`, with those components deleted; the result has length `n − r`.
For a code `C` ⊆ `R⁽ⁿ⁾` and elements `a₁,…,aₙ ∈ R`: the codeword `(a₁,…,aₙ)` of `C`. It is checked that the vector lies in `C`.
For a code `C` ⊆ `V = R⁽ⁿ⁾` and `u ∈ V`: the codeword of `C` corresponding to `u`. Fails if `u ∉ C`.
The zero word of `C`.
Sum of codewords `u`, `v` of the same linear code `C`.
Additive inverse of the codeword `u` of `C`.
Difference of codewords `u`, `v` of the same linear code `C`.
For `a ∈ R` and codeword `u ∈ C`: the codeword `a∗u`.
The Hamming weight of `v` (number of non-zero components).
The Hamming distance between codewords `u`, `v` of the same code `C`.
For a word `w` of the length `n` code `C`: its support as a subset of `{1..n}` (the coordinates where `w` is non-zero).
Inner product of vectors `u`, `v` (Euclidean norm), both in the parent vector space of `C`.
For a length `n` linear code `C` and codeword `u`: the coordinates of `u` with respect to `C`, as `Q = [a₁,…,a_k]` over the alphabet with `u = a₁∗C.1 + … + a_k∗C.k`.

For an element `u` of a code over `R`: the normalization of `u` — the unique `v = a·u` (scalar `a ∈ R`) whose first non-zero entry is the canonical associate in `R` of the first non-zero entry of `u` (`v` is zero if `u` is zero).
The vector obtained from `u` by cyclically shifting its components to the right by `k` positions.
Destructively rotate `u` by `k` positions.
For a word `w` of the code `C`: the ambient space `V` of `C`.
For a codeword `u` of `C` over `R`: the `i`-th component of `u` (as an element of `R`).
For `u` in a subcode `C` of the full `R`-space `V = Rⁿ`, `1 ≤ i ≤ n`, and `x ∈ R`: a vector in `V` equal to `u` with its `i`-th component redefined to be `x`.

`true` iff `C` is (resp. is not) a subcode of `D`.
`true` iff the codes `C` and `D` are equal (resp. not equal).

`true` iff `C` is self-dual, i.e. `C` equals the dual of `C`.
`true` iff `C` is self-orthogonal, i.e. `C` is contained in the dual of `C`.
`true` iff the (non-quantum) code `C` is projective.

description: For a field `F`, subfield `K ⊆ F` and positive integer `n`: the `[n, 0, n]` code consisting of only the zero codeword (minimum weight conventionally taken to be `n`).
The `[n, 1, n]` `K`-additive code over `F` consisting of all repeating codewords.
The `[n, n−1, 2]` `K`-additive code over `F` of all codewords `(c_1,…,c_n)` with `Σ_i c_i = 0`.
The `[n, n, 1]` `K`-additive code over `F` consisting of all possible codewords.

The block length `n` of `C`.

The number of codewords belonging to `C`.
The information rate `k/n` of the `[n, k]` code `C`.

A random codeword of `C`.

For a word `w` of `C`: the ambient space `V` of `C`.
The vector obtained from `u` by cyclically shifting its components to the right by `k` positions.

description: The weight distribution of `C`, returned as a sequence of tuples whose `i`-th tuple `<w_i, n_i>` gives a weight and the number of codewords of that weight.

The complete weight enumerator `W_C(z_0,…,z_{q−1})` for `C`, where `q = #E` is the size of the alphabet `E`. With the `q` elements `ω_0,…,ω_{q−1}` (for a prime field `ω_i = i`; otherwise `ω_0 = 0`, `ω_i = α^{i−1}` for `α` primitive), and `s_i(u)` the number of components of `u` equal to `ω_i`, it is `Σ_{u∈C} z_0^{s_0(u)} … z_{q−1}^{s_{q−1}(u)}`.

The set of all words of the linear code `C` having weight between `l` and `u` inclusive. Parameters: `Cutoff` (`RngIntElt`, default ∞), `StoreWords` (`BoolElt`, default `true`) — if `true`, any words of a single weight generated are stored internally.

For a single vector `v` or a sequence `Q` of vectors over a finite field `F`: the `K`-additive code over `F` generated by all shifts of the inputs. `K ⊆ F`; if `K` is the prime subfield of `F` it may be omitted.

description: For a single polynomial `f` or sequence `Q` of polynomials over a finite field `F`: the `K`-additive code of length `n` over `F` generated by all shifts of the inputs. `K ⊆ F`; may be omitted if `K` is the prime subfield.

For two vectors of equal length `n`, `v4` over `GF(4)` and `v2` over `GF(2)`: the `F2`-additive code generated by all cyclic shifts of both. For `GF(2)`-additive codes over `GF(4)`, two generators suffice for any such code.

For two polynomials `f4` over `GF(4)` and `f2` over `GF(2)` (degrees not exceeding `n−1`): the `F2`-additive code of length `n` generated by all cyclic shifts of both. Two generators suffice for any `GF(2)`-additive code over `GF(4)`.

For an integer `n` and a sequence `Q` of polynomials over a finite field `F`: the `K`-additive quasicyclic code whose cyclic blocks are generated by the polynomials in `Q`. `K ⊆ F`; may be omitted if `K` is the prime subfield.
As above, but the cyclic blocks are stacked 2-dimensionally to height `h`.
For a sequence `Q` of vectors over a finite field `F`: the `K`-additive quasicyclic code whose cyclic blocks are generated by the vectors in `Q`. `K ⊆ F`; may be omitted if prime subfield.
As above, with the cyclic blocks stacked 2-dimensionally to height `h`.
A new additive code formed by including the all-ones vector with the words of `C`.
For a subcode `S` of `C`: a code `C'` such that `C = S + C'`. Both `C` and `S` must be over the same field.
The direct sum of `C` and `D`: all vectors `u|v` with `u ∈ C`, `v ∈ D`.
For a sequence `Q = [C_1,…,C_r]` of codes over the same field `F`: the direct sum of the `C_i`.

For an `[n_1, k_1]` code `C` and an `[n_2, k_2]` code `D` over the same ring `R`: the direct product, of length `n_1·n_2`, whose generator matrix is the Kronecker product of the basis matrices of `C` and `D`.
For an `[n, k, d]` additive code `C`: a new code `C'` formed by adding the extra coordinate to each vector making the coordinate sum zero.
The code obtained by extending `C` `n` times.
Add `n` zeros to the end of each codeword of `C`.
For `C1`, `C2` over the same alphabet: the code of all vectors `u|u+v` with `u ∈ C1`, `v ∈ C2`. Zeros are appended to reconcile length differences.

For `C1`, `C2`, `C3` over the same alphabet `K`: the code of all vectors `u|u+a*v|u+v+w` with `u ∈ C1`, `v ∈ C2`, `w ∈ C3`. Parameter `a` (`FldFinElt`, default −1 ⇒ a primitive element of `K`) is the multiplier. Zeros are appended to equalise codeword lengths.
For an `[n, k]` code `C` and `1 ≤ i ≤ n`: a new code `C'` formed by deleting the `i`-th coordinate from each codeword.
For an `[n, k]` code `C` and a set `S = {i_1,…,i_r}` of distinct integers in `[1, n]`: a new code formed by deleting components `i_1,…,i_r` from each codeword.
For an `[n, k]` code `C` and `1 ≤ i ≤ n`: the code formed by selecting codewords of `C` having a zero in the `i`-th component and deleting that component (resulting length `n−1`).

For an `[n, k]` code `C` and a set `S = {i_1,…,i_r}` of distinct integers in `[1, n]`: the code formed by selecting codewords with zeros in each position `i_1,…,i_r` and deleting those components (resulting length `n−r`).
For `C1`, `C2` over the same field `K`: the concatenation `C` of `C1` and `C2`; the generators of `C` are the concatenations of the generators of `C1` and `C2`.

For an `[n_1, k, d_1]` code `C1` and an `[n_2, k, d_2]` code `C2` of the same dimension over the same field `K`: an `[n_1 + n_2, k, ≥ d_1 + d_2]` code whose generator matrix is `HorizontalJoin(A, B)` (`A`, `B` the generator matrices of `C1`, `C2`).
The automorphism group of the additive code `C`. Currently only available for additive codes over `GF(4)`.
The subgroup of the automorphism group of `C` consisting of permutations of the coordinates. Currently only available for additive codes over `GF(4)`.

Given an additive code `S` self-orthogonal with respect to the symplectic inner product, return the quantum code defined by `S`. Parameter `ExtendedFormat` (default `false`): when `false`, `S` is a length-n additive code over GF(q²) (compact); when `true`, `S` is a length-2n additive code over GF(q) (extended).

Given a matrix `M` over GF(q²) whose GF(q)-additive row span is a symplectic self-orthogonal code `S`, return the quantum code defined by `S`. Parameter `ExtendedFormat` (default `false`): compact (length-n rows over GF(q²)) vs extended (length-2n rows over GF(q)).
algorithm: Builds `S` from the additive span of the rows of `M`, then **[CRSS98]**.

description: Given a graph `G`, return the self-dual (dimension 0) quantum code defined by the adjacency matrix of `G`.
For `F` a degree-2 extension of GF(q) and positive integers `n ≥ k`, return a random `[[n, k]]` quantum stabilizer code over `F`. `F` is assumed in compact format.
Given a quantum code `Q` of dimension `k_Q ≥ k`, return a subcode of `Q` of dimension `k`.
Return the `[[6, 0, 4]]` self-dual quantum hexacode.
Return the `[[12, 0, 6]]` self-dual quantum dodecacode.
Given two classical linear binary codes `C1` and `C2` of length n with `C2` a subcode of `C1`, form a quantum code using the Calderbank–Shor–Steane construction.

Parameter `LinearSpan` (default `false`): additive span over prime field vs linear span if `true`.

For GF(2)-additive codes over GF(4): given `v4` over GF(4) and `v2` over GF(2), both of length n, return the length-n code generated by the additive span of their cyclic shifts. The span must be symplectic self-orthogonal.

Given an integer `n` and a sequence `Q` of polynomials over a finite field `F`, let `S` be the quasi-cyclic classical code generated by the span of the vectors formed by concatenating cyclic blocks generated by the polynomials in `Q`. If `S` is symplectic self-orthogonal, return the quasi-cyclic quantum code with stabiliser code `S` (else an error). Parameter `LinearSpan` (default `false`): additive span over the prime field, or linear span if `true`.

Given a sequence `Q` of vectors, return the quantum code whose additive stabiliser matrix is constructed from the length-n cyclic blocks generated by the cyclic shifts of the vectors in `Q`. Parameter `LinearSpan` (default `false`): linear span if `true`, additive span otherwise.
Given a degree-2 extension field `F = GF(q²)`, return the element λ ∈ F connecting the extended and compact formats: a vector `(a|b)` in extended format corresponds to `w = a + λb` in compact format.
The additive stabiliser code `S` defining the quantum code `Q`. Parameter `ExtendedFormat` (default `false`): compact length-n code over GF(q²), or extended length-2n code over GF(q) if `true`.

The additive normalizer matrix `M` defining `Q`. Parameter `ExtendedFormat` (default `false`): compact vs extended.

Return the abelian group representing all possible errors for a length-n p-ary qubit system: an extra-special group of order `p^(2n+1)` with `2n + 1` generators corresponding to the qubit-flip operators `X(i)`, phase-flip operators `Z(i)`, and overall phase multiplication `W` by the p-th root of unity. Return the abelian group representing all possible errors on a length-n binary qubit system: an extra-special group of order `2^(2n-1)`.

Return the abelian group of errors defining `Q`, a subgroup of `QuantumErrorGroup(Q)`.
Given `Q` with error group `G` (an extra-special group), return the abelian group of errors of `Q` as a subgroup of `G`.

For `v1, v2` in `K^(n)` (`K` a finite field), return their symplectic inner product. In extended format `(a|b) * (c|d) = ad − bc`; for binary codes whose compact format is over GF(4), it is `Trace(v1 · v̄2)`. Parameter `ExtendedFormat` (default `false`).

The dual of the additive (or linear) code `C` with respect to the symplectic inner product. Parameter `ExtendedFormat` (default `false`): compact length-n code over GF(q²) vs extended length-2n code over GF(q).
Return `true` if `C` equals its symplectic dual. Parameter `ExtendedFormat` (default `false`).
Return `true` if `C` is contained in its symplectic dual. Parameter `ExtendedFormat` (default `false`).

Given `[[n₁, k₁, d₁]]` and `[[n₂, k₂, d₂]]` quantum codes, return the `[[n₁+n₂, k₁+k₂, min{d₁,d₂}]]` quantum code which is their direct product.
Given an `[[n, k, d]]` quantum code `Q`, return the extended `[[n+1, k, d]]` quantum code.
Perform `m` extensions on the `[[n, k, d]]` quantum code `Q`, returning the extended `[[n+m, k, d]]` quantum code.

Given `[[n, k, d]]` quantum code `Q` and a set `I` of coordinate positions of size `s`, return the `[[n−s, k' >= k−s, d' >= d]]` quantum code produced by shortening at the positions in `I`. May give an error if not valid.

Return the best known upper bound on the minimum distance of `[[n, k]]` quantum codes over `F`. Available for binary quantum codes (`F = GF(4)`) up to length 35.

The subgroup of the automorphism group of `Q` consisting of those automorphisms which permute the coordinates of codewords. Currently only applies to binary quantum codes.

Computes the first `t` sequence elements of the LFSR with connection polynomial `C` and initial state the sequence `S` (so the LFSR length is the length of `S`). `C` must be at least degree 1, its coefficients must come from the same finite field as the universe of `S`, and its constant coefficient must be 1. `S` must have at least as many terms as the degree of `C`.
Computes the next state of the LFSR having connection polynomial `C` and current state `S` (the LFSR length is the length of `S`). Same constraints on `C` and `S` as `LFSRSequence`.
algorithm: Single application of the LFSR recurrence.

description: Given a sequence `S` of elements from `F_q`, returns the connection polynomial `C(D)` and the length `L` of an LFSR that generates `S`. Note that `BerlekampMassey` may return a singular LFSR (i.e. deg `C(D)` less than `L`); one must therefore use the first `L` elements of `S` to regenerate the sequence.

Outputs a sequence of `t` bits from the shrinking generator having connection polynomials `C₁` and `C₂` and initial state sequences `S₁` and `S₂` (so the LFSR lengths are the lengths of `S₁` and `S₂`). Bits are elements of **F₂**. Polynomial coefficients and sequence elements must be from **F₂**; the connection polynomials must have degree at least 1 with trailing coefficient 1; each initial state must have at least as many elements as the degree of the corresponding connection polynomial.

Generates a sequence of `t` bits using the RSA pseudo-random bit generator with an RSA modulus of approximately `b` bits in length. The modulus `n` is computed by finding (pseudo-)random primes with `RandomPrime`. If `gcd(φ(n), 3)` is 1, the exponent 3 is used; otherwise a (pseudo-)random exponent `e` is chosen with `gcd(φ(n), e) = 1`. The seed is chosen as a (pseudo-)random number modulo `n`. Bits are elements of **F₂**.
Generates a sequence of `t` bits using the RSA pseudo-random bit generator with modulus `n`, exponent `e`, and seed value `s`. Bits are elements of **F₂**. `n` must be larger than 1.

Returns an RSA modulus `n` of `b` bits in length, and an exponent `e` such that `Gcd(EulerPhi(n), e) = 1`. The values can be used with `RandomSequenceRSA`. `b` must be at least 16. *Warning:* not for real-world cryptographic use.
algorithm: Random-prime construction of an RSA modulus.

description: Returns an RSA modulus `n` of `b` bits in length such that `Gcd(EulerPhi(n), e) = 1`, for use with the supplied exponent `e` and `RandomSequenceRSA`. `b` must be at least 16; `e` must be odd and in the range `1 < e < 2^b`. *Warning:* not for real-world cryptographic use.

Generates a sequence of `t` bits using the Blum–Blum–Shub pseudo-random bit generator with a modulus of approximately `b` bits in length. The modulus `n` is computed by finding (pseudo-)random primes with `RandomPrime` (with the condition that the primes are congruent to 3 mod 4). The seed is a (pseudo-)random number modulo `n`. Bits are elements of **F₂**. `b` must be at least 16.

Generates a sequence of `t` bits using the Blum–Blum–Shub pseudo-random bit generator with modulus `n` and seed value `s`. Bits are elements of **F₂**. `n` must be larger than 1 and `gcd(s, n)` must be 1.
Returns a Blum–Blum–Shub modulus `b` bits in length, for use with `RandomSequenceBlumBlumShub`. `b` must be at least 16. *Warning:* not for real-world cryptographic use.
algorithm: Random-prime construction of a Blum–Blum–Shub modulus.

description: Computes the autocorrelation of a sequence `S` (universe **F₂**), defined as `C(t) = Σ_{i=1}^{L} (−1)^{S[i]+S[i+t]}`, where `L` is the length of the sequence and the values of `S[i+t]` wrap around to the beginning when `i+t > L`.
algorithm: Direct evaluation of the autocorrelation sum with wrap-around.

description: Computes the crosscorrelation of two binary sequences `S₁` and `S₂` (each with universe **F₂**, and the same length `L`), defined as `C(t) = Σ_{i=1}^{L} (−1)^{S₁[i]+S₂[i+t]}`, with `S₂[i+t]` wrapping around to the beginning when `i+t > L`.
algorithm: Direct evaluation of the crosscorrelation sum with wrap-around.

description: Given a binary sequence `S` and integers `f` and `d`, returns the decimation of `S`: the sequence containing elements `S[f], S[f+d], S[f+2d], …` where the indices in `S` are interpreted with wrap-around as integers between 1 and `#S`.
algorithm: Index sampling with stride `d`, offset `f`, wrap-around.

description: Decimation of `S` returning a new sequence containing the first `t` elements of `S[f], S[f+d], S[f+2d], …`, indices interpreted with wrap-around between 1 and `#S`.
